instances.label: Inpatient rehab or acute hospital: before discharge, the OT trains a spouse or adult child in safe transfers, bed mobility, ADL assistance, precautions and equipment use — explaining, demonstrating, watching a return demonstration and giving corrective feedback and written instructions.

Home health visit: the OT instructs a family caregiver in the patient's home program, adaptive equipment use, bathing/dressing assistance, home-safety routines and what to do between visits, tailored to that household's setup.

Pediatric setting (early intervention, school, or outpatient clinic): the OT teaches parents, foster caregivers or classroom aides positioning, handling, sensory and feeding strategies, splint wear schedules, and carryover activities to continue after the session.

Skilled nursing / long-term care facility: the OT trains CNAs and restorative nursing staff in positioning, contracture management, splint application schedules, self-feeding setup and safe assist levels for a specific resident, and documents the training.

Outpatient clinic (hand therapy, ortho, neuro): the OT instructs the accompanying caregiver or spouse in a home exercise program, orthosis wear and care, wound/edema precautions, and warning signs to report, using handouts, photos or video.

tasks.label: Lay out materials such as puzzles, scissors and eating utensils for use in therapy, and clean and repair these tools after therapy sessions.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Outpatient/inpatient rehab clinic OT gym: before a scheduled patient, the OT pulls fine-motor and ADL items from labeled bins and shelves (pegboards, puzzles, therapy putty, adapted scissors, coins, clothespins) and lays them out on a mat table or work surface within the patient's reach per the treatment plan; after the session she gathers the items, wipes each with a disinfectant wipe per infection-control policy, and returns them to the correct storage bin.

Hospital or skilled nursing facility ADL kitchen/bedside: OT sets out adaptive eating utensils, built-up spoons, plate guard, nosey cup, dishes and a napkin for a self-feeding or meal-prep session; afterward washes the utensils and dishes at the sink or in the dishwasher, sanitizes them, dries and restocks the ADL cart or cupboard.

School-based OT: loads a therapy bag or rolling cart, brings it to a classroom or shared therapy room with children present, lays out scissors, paper, pencil grips, manipulatives and sensory tools for the student on a desk or floor mat; collects and wipes items between students, repacks the bag and restocks consumables.

Home health / early-intervention visit in a client's private home: OT unpacks a kit onto the family's kitchen table or living-room floor amid household clutter, pets and furniture that differ every visit, sets out utensils, puzzles or dressing aids; then repacks, wipes items with sanitizer, and stores the kit in the car.

Clinic workroom between sessions: inspection, deep cleaning and repair of therapy tools — soaking/washing toys and putty tools, replacing worn Velcro straps and splint parts, gluing or replacing broken puzzle pieces, tightening or adjusting loop scissors and switch toys, changing batteries, restringing beads, identifying missing pieces and rebuilding kits.

sources.title: Introducing Helix 02: Full-Body Autonomy
sources.claim: Figure's Helix 02 ran a continuous four-minute autonomous loco-manipulation task in a full-sized kitchen: walking to the dishwasher, unloading dishes, stacking items in cabinets, then ....
sources.transferJustification: Related task: kitchen dish handling. It covers the same object class as the eating-utensil and dish instance (cups, plates, utensils), the same put-away-into-designated-storage step as returning therapy tools to bins, and comparable grasp precision without breakage, in a walk-around room rather than a fixture.

sources.title: Figure's Humanoid Robot Picks Up Toys, Wipes Surfaces in New Demo
sources.claim: A Figure humanoid running Helix 02 autonomously tidied a cluttered living room, picking ... toys and other objects, spraying a surface and wiping it with a towel, and re-holstering the towel on its arm to free its hands.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: room tidying with cleaning-tool use. Picking up scattered toys and putting them away is the same pick-and-place over small, varied, non-rigid-to-rigid objects as collecting puzzles, utensils and manipulatives; spray-and-wipe with a cloth is the same motion as disinfectant wipe-down of tools and work surfaces.

sources.title: A VLA with Open-World Generalization (pi-0.5)
sources.claim: Physical Intelligence's pi-0.5 controlled a mobile manipulator to clean ... kitchens and bedrooms in homes never seen in training, performing long-horizon manipulation such as putting dishes in the sink and objects into drawers.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: cleaning up an unfamiliar room. It substantiates generalization of grasping and put-away over varied household objects and layouts, which is what varies between clinic treatment rooms and therapy kits, though success is research-grade rather than deployment-grade.

sources.title: pi*0.6: a VLA That Learns From Experience
sources.claim: Physical Intelligence's pi*0.6 with RECAP ran uninterrupted for hours on multi-step manipulation: folding novel laundry in a real home, assembling factory boxes, and making espresso drinks on a professional machine, roughly doubling throughput and halving failures.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: hours-long repeated manipulation routines. It speaks to the reliability and throughput dimension of 'worker quality' for repetitive set-up/clean-up cycles with varied items, not to therapy materials specifically.

sources.title: Diligent Robotics Unveils Moxi 2.0
sources.claim: Diligent Robotics' Moxi mobile manipulator operates autonomously in more than 25 US ..., fetching and delivering supplies, specimens and pharmacy items through corridors, elevators and supply rooms, with over one million deliveries completed.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: fetching and returning supplies inside a clinical facility. It substantiates the navigation, storage-room access and item transport half of the instance at true deployment scale in an E2 healthcare setting, though its manipulation is limited to totes and bags.

sources.system: Autonomous instrument tray assembly cell (YOLO12 + ResNet perception, magnetic gripper)
sources.title: Towards Autonomous Instrument Tray Assembly for Sterile Processing Applications
sources.claim: A fully automated robotic system sorts surgical instruments and packs them into sterile trays in fixed, divider-defined positions, using vision-based fine-grained instrument classification, with fewer tool-to-tool collisions than human-assembled trays.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: laying out hand tools in prescribed positions. Surgical instruments are the same size and rigidity class as scissors, utensils and small manipulatives, and correct identification plus placement into a defined layout is exactly the 'lay out materials' step, here done in a purpose-built cell with 3D-printed holders (E1).

sources.title: Dishcraft Robotics Automatically Cleans Dishes and Utensils
sources.claim: Dishcraft Robotics' machine-vision dishwashing system autonomously scrubbed dishes and utensils in commercial kitchens serving corporate food service, cleaning roughly 100 dishes at a time after staff loaded them onto carts.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: machine washing of eating utensils and dishes. It substantiates the 'clean these tools after sessions' step for utensils in a purpose-built machine where the work is brought to the machine on custom carts (E1).

sources.title: This robot will clean toilets for $1,000 a month
sources.claim: Somatic's cleaning robot autonomously disinfects, mops and vacuum-dries surfaces in office-building restrooms after the floor plan is mapped, and is sold as an installed service to facilities.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous spray-and-wipe disinfection inside a structured human facility. It shows disinfectant application and wiping to an institutional cleaning standard in an E2 building, though on fixtures rather than on individual hand-held tools.

sources.title: TidyBot: personalized robot assistance with large language models (Autonomous Robots)
sources.claim: TidyBot, a real mobile manipulator, put away 85% of objects correctly in real-world room cleanup tests, choosing the right storage location for each object using an LLM-derived preference model.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: putting varied objects into their designated storage places. This is the 'return tools to the right bin after therapy' step; the 85% rate indicates the capability exists but is below the error rate an employer would accept without supervision.

tasks.label: Design and create, or requisition, special supplies and equipment, such as splints, braces, and computer-aided adaptive equipment.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Outpatient hand-therapy or inpatient rehab clinic: OT fabricates a custom upper-extremity orthosis (wrist cock-up, resting hand splint, thumb spica) for a specific patient — draws a pattern, heats low-temperature thermoplastic, molds it directly on the patient's limb, trims, rivets straps, checks bony prominences and skin, and adjusts at follow-up.

Clinic fabrication room or bedside: OT designs and makes a small custom adaptive aid that can be specified geometrically — a built-up grip/utensil holder, key turner, pen grip, custom switch or device mount, page turner — increasingly by CAD plus a clinic 3D printer, then issues it to the client.

Hospital, SNF, school or outpatient clinic: OT requisitions commercially available equipment (tub bench, reacher, wheelchair cushion, adaptive keyboard, sock aid) — selects the product from vendor/stock catalogs, completes the order or letter of medical necessity, and the item is pulled from central supply or a distributor and brought to the client.

Clinic, school or workstation: OT sets up computer-aided adaptive equipment — mounts a switch or AAC device on a wheelchair with clamps and tools, positions it to the client's reliable movement, programs/configures the software, and re-adjusts with the client seated in the chair.

Client's home, school classroom or workplace: OT improvises a custom adaptation on site with hand tools and shop materials — foam tubing and Velcro on existing utensils or tools, a cut-down reacher, a foam positioning wedge, a switch-adapted toy, a modified doorknob or drawer pull — fitted and trialed in place.

sources.system: ActivArmor (Scan app + Designware cloud design + desktop 3D printer)
sources.title: Become A Provider | ActivArmor | Custom 3D Printed Casts and Splints
sources.claim: ActivArmor supplies clinics with a scan app, cloud design software and 3D printer so a custom-fit cast/splint is machine-designed from a phone scan and printed at point of care; devices are FDA-listed Class 1 splints used commercially for years.

sources.title: ActivArmor Casts and Splints Are Shifting to Point-of-Care 3D Printing | Additive Manufacturing
sources.claim: Trade press confirms the ActivArmor package lets medical facilities produce custom 3D-printed casts and splints in hours, with the company designing and printing devices from clinician-captured scan data.

sources.title: 3D-Printed Hand Splints versus Thermoplastic Splints: A Randomized Controlled Pilot Feasibility Trial
sources.claim: A randomized controlled pilot trial found machine-fabricated (3D-printed) hand splints made from a surface scan achieved patient satisfaction comparable to conventionally molded thermoplastic splints, supporting worker-quality equivalence of the fabricated output.

sources.title: phits: The World's First Dynamic 3D-Printed Orthotics
sources.claim: Materialise Phits runs a digital-order-to-production workflow in which a clinician's patient data file is sent to an industrial additive manufacturing facility that produces the custom orthotic device.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: fabricating a custom foot orthosis from patient measurement data. It transfers to splint/brace fabrication because it is the same class of custom-fit, body-worn orthotic device, made to comparable millimetre fit tolerances by computer-controlled fabrication in a purpose-built production facility.

sources.title: Moxi — Diligent Robotics
sources.claim: Moxi mobile manipulators work autonomously inside hospitals fetching items from central supply ... delivering supplies, medications and lab samples to clinical units.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: retrieving requisitioned items from hospital central supply and conveying them to the unit where they are needed. This is the physical content of an equipment requisition — the same standard-sized supply items moved along the same institutional routes.

sources.title: Diligent Robotics completes 300,000 pharmacy deliveries with Moxi - The Robot Report
sources.claim: Diligent's Moxi fleet has completed over one million autonomous deliveries in more than 25 US ..., including 300,000 pharmacy deliveries and 100,000 autonomous elevator rides.
sources.transferJustification: Same as above: substantiates reliability and scale of autonomous in-facility retrieval and delivery of requisitioned medical items.

sources.title: RightHand Robotics | Pharmaceutical
sources.claim: RightHand Robotics' RightPick piece-picking system fills pharmaceutical and healthcare orders autonomously around the clock with minimal ..., and is deployed at customers including Apotea and Staples.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: filling an order by picking individual stocked items. Requisitioning adaptive equipment resolves physically to picking catalogue items of comparable size and fragility from stock, which this system does autonomously in a controlled facility.

sources.system: Makers Making Change assistive device library + consumer/desktop 3D printers
sources.title: 3D Printing Assistive Technology and the Future Ahead
sources.claim: Open-source libraries of 3D-printable assistive devices (key turners, utensil grips, page ..., switch-adapted toys) are used by occupational therapists and makers, with the device produced by a 3D printer from the design file.

sources.title: New auto ejection tool for Bambu Lab print farms automatically ejects finished 3D prints from the machine
sources.claim: Commercial auto-ejection kits let desktop 3D print farms run unattended, removing finished parts and starting the next job without an operator between prints.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: unattended production of printed parts. It shows the fabrication step for splints and adaptive aids can run with limited intervention rather than an operator handling each build.

roles.title: Low Vision Therapists, Orientation and Mobility Specialists, and Vision Rehabilitation Therapists
aliases: Blind Orientation and Mobility Therapist (Blind O and M Therapist)
Orientation and Mobility Instructor (O and M Instructor)
Orientation and Mobility Specialist (O and M Specialist)
roles.description: Provide therapy to patients with visual impairments to improve their functioning in daily life activities. May train patients in activities such as computer use, communication skills, or home management skills.

tasks.label: Teach cane skills, including cane use with a guide, diagonal techniques, and two-point touches.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Indoor instruction at a vision-rehab agency, VA blind rehabilitation center, or clinic: instructor physically shapes the client's grip and wrist position, models the diagonal technique hand-under-hand, walks beside a novice adult client down corridors, through doorways and stairwells, physically blocks/guards to prevent collisions and falls, and corrects arc width and rhythm in real time.

School-based instruction with a blind child: teaching two-point touch and diagonal technique in hallways, cafeteria, stairwells and campus grounds; frequent physical prompts (touch of elbow, repositioning hand), constant proximity guarding of a distractible young learner, sessions fitted around class traffic.

In-home instruction with an adult or elderly client, often with comorbidities (balance issues, neuropathy, hearing loss): teaching cane-with-guide (client grips the instructor's arm), diagonal technique in cluttered rooms, negotiating porch steps, thresholds and the driveway; instructor physically supports and steadies the client.

Quiet residential neighborhood lessons: two-point touch along uneven sidewalks, shorelining grass lines, detecting curbs and driveway slopes, recovering from veering; instructor shadows a half-step behind, intervenes physically when the client drifts toward the roadway or an obstacle.

Busy commercial/urban travel lessons: crowded sidewalks, construction detours, street crossings, bus and rail platforms; instructor monitors traffic and pedestrians, gives immediate verbal and tactile corrections, and physically stops the client at the curb or in a hazardous situation.

sources.developer: Stanford University (Patrick Slade, Mykel Kochenderfer et al.)
sources.title: Multimodal sensing and intuitive steering assistance improve navigation and mobility for people with impaired vision | Science Robotics
sources.claim: The Augmented Cane is a handheld robotic navigation aid that senses the environment and steers a blind traveler via a motorized roller tip; it assists a traveler's own mobility but does not instruct, assess, or physically correct a learner's cane technique.
sources.transferJustification: Related task = assistive travel guidance for a blind user. It does not transfer to teaching cane skills: the device substitutes for the traveler's sensing rather than teaching a motor technique, and it performs no assessment of grip, arc width, rhythm, or hand-under-hand correction.

sources.title: Navigating Real-World Challenges: A Quadruped Robot Guiding System for Visually Impaired People in Diverse Environments (CHI 2024)
sources.claim: Research quadruped guide-dog robots lead blind and visually impaired users along routes with leash/kinesthetic feedback in indoor and outdoor trials, but they are guiding devices evaluated with users, not instructors that teach and correct white-cane technique.
sources.transferJustification: Related task = physically guiding a blind pedestrian. Transfer fails because guiding replaces the traveler's own technique, whereas the task requires diagnosing errors in a learner's cane stroke, providing tactile modeling, and guarding safety while the learner travels independently.

sources.system: Socially Assistive Robot (SAR) exercise coach (Bandit platform)
sources.title: A Socially Assistive Robot Exercise Coach for the Elderly — Journal of Human-Robot Interaction
sources.claim: Socially assistive robots can autonomously run coaching sessions for simple physical exercises with older adults, demonstrating and verbally encouraging movements, but such systems work with seated/standing sighted users in controlled study rooms and provide no physical contact, tactile shaping, or mobility safety guarding.
sources.transferJustification: Related task = robot-led motor-skill coaching. Transfer fails: coaching relies on the user watching the robot's demonstration and on gross pose tracking, while cane instruction for a blind learner requires hands-on shaping of grip and arc, judging tactile feedback the learner receives, and physically preventing falls and traffic hazards.

tasks.label: Recommend appropriate mobility devices or systems, such as human guides, dog guides, long canes, electronic travel aids (ETAs), and other adaptive mobility devices (AMDs).

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

tasks.label: Train clients with visual impairments to use mobility devices or systems, such as human guides, dog guides, electronic travel aids (ETAs), and other adaptive mobility devices (AMDs).

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Long-cane / adaptive mobility device skills instruction indoors at a rehab center, hospital, or agency training unit: the specialist positions the client's hand on the grip, models and physically shapes the arc and two-point-touch rhythm through guided touch, corrects body alignment, walks beside the client through hallways, doorways and stairwells, and physically blocks collisions with furniture and people.

Cane travel and route instruction in the client's own community: residential sidewalks, business districts, uncontrolled and signalized street crossings, bus stops and transit boarding, in variable weather, traffic and construction. The specialist shadows the traveler at a distance, reads traffic, gives verbal correction, and physically intervenes to prevent a step into the roadway.

Human (sighted) guide technique training: the specialist acts as the guide with the client gripping just above the elbow, teaching transitions to narrow passages, doorways, stairs, seating and vehicles; also coaching family members or aides to guide correctly, usually in the client's home and immediate neighborhood.

Electronic travel aid / wearable / GPS app training: fitting and calibrating a smart cane, ultrasonic or camera-based wearable, or navigation app, teaching the client to interpret audio and haptic cues and to combine the device with cane technique, first in a controlled indoor space and then on real outdoor routes.

Dog guide-related instruction: pre-dog readiness work, orienting a returning dog guide handler to new routes, workplaces or campuses, and troubleshooting handling problems (traffic checks, curb work, escalators) alongside the working team on public streets.

Pediatric or multiple-disability clients in a school or early-intervention setting: pre-cane and protective techniques, adapted mobility devices (hoops, push devices, support canes), taught with hand-under-hand prompting, physical positioning, and constant physical safeguarding of a child who may resist or bolt.

sources.title: GuideNav: User-Informed Development of a Vision-Only Robotic Navigation Assistant For Blind Travelers
sources.claim: GuideNav is a vision-only quadruped/robotic navigation assistant that autonomously guided blind and low-vision travelers along outdoor routes in user studies; it substitutes for a guide (leads the traveler) rather than teaching the traveler mobility technique.
sources.transferJustification: Related task = guiding a blind traveler outdoors. It does not transfer to this task: the system performs the travel for the user, and provides no assessment of the client's grip, cane arc, protective technique or route-learning, and no hands-on correction or lesson sequencing, which are the deliverables of mobility-device training.

sources.title: Field Trials of Autonomous Navigation Robot for Visually Impaired People
sources.claim: The AI Suitcase is an ... for visually impaired users that has been in permanent daily operation guiding visitors inside the Miraikan museum since April 2024 — a guiding deployment inside a controlled institutional facility, not instruction of clients in mobility technique.
sources.transferJustification: Related task = guiding BVI people through an indoor institutional space. It does not transfer: the robot navigates for the user; museum staff, not the robot, orient users to the device, and the robot cannot evaluate or physically correct a learner's mobility skills or supervise street travel.

sources.system: Socially assistive robots (e.g., NAO-based exercise coaches)
sources.title: Use of Socially Assistive Robots in Physiotherapy: Scoping Review
sources.claim: Socially assistive robots used in physiotherapy provide verbal/social feedback and exercise coaching in research studies; reviews report small samples and technical limitations, and these platforms provide no hands-on physical guidance or safety intervention.
sources.transferJustification: Related task = coaching a patient through rehabilitation exercises. Does not transfer: coaching is verbal/demonstrative with a sighted, stationary patient in a clinic, whereas mobility-device training requires guided-touch hand shaping, acting as a physical human guide, and mobile safety shadowing of a blind traveler.

tasks.label: Develop rehabilitation or instructional plans collaboratively with clients, based on results of assessments, needs, and goals.

tasks.label: Write reports or complete forms to document assessments, training, progress, or follow-up outcomes.

tasks.label: Train clients to use tactile, auditory, kinesthetic, olfactory, and proprioceptive information.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Community O&M lesson with an adult who is newly blind: on residential sidewalks, at bus stops and signalized crossings, the specialist teaches the client to interpret traffic sound patterns, cane tip feedback on texture/slope changes, wind and sun orientation, and smell landmarks (bakery, exhaust), physically repositioning the client's body/cane arm as needed and safeguarding at the curb. Weather, pedestrians, parked cars and construction vary each session.

In-home vision rehabilitation therapy session: teaching the client to use tactile bump dots and raised markings on appliance dials, tactile/olfactory cues for identifying food and cleaning products, kinesthetic memory for pouring and knife work, and proprioceptive body awareness for moving safely through their own furnished rooms; includes hand-under-hand demonstration and setting up tactile materials on the client's own equipment.

Indoor travel/sensory-skills lesson inside a rehabilitation center, hospital, school or office building: teaching trailing along walls, detecting doorways and intersecting corridors from air movement and echo, using HVAC hum, elevator chimes and floor-surface changes as landmarks, with hand-under-hand guidance on the wall/handrail and immediate corrective feedback.

Pediatric or deafblind instruction in a school or early-intervention classroom: hand-under-hand tactile exploration of objects and tactile symbols, body-part and spatial concept work, sound-localization games, prompting hierarchies faded over sessions, with physical positioning of the child's hands, trunk and feet and management of tactile defensiveness.

Clinic-based low vision therapy session at a table: teaching a client with severe central field loss non-visual compensations alongside residual vision - tactile identification of medication bottles and money, auditory scanning with talking devices, olfactory and texture cues for household products - with demonstration, guided practice and correction.

sources.developer: Carnegie Mellon University / IBM Research (Asakawa group)
sources.title: CaBot: Designing and Evaluating an Autonomous Navigation Robot for Blind People
sources.claim: CaBot is an autonomous suitcase-shaped robot that guides blind users to destinations while avoiding obstacles; it substitutes for a guide, it does not teach a client to interpret tactile, auditory or proprioceptive cues, and it does not assess or shape client skill.
sources.transferJustification: Closest robotic system operating with blind travellers in the same environments as O&M lessons; cited to show the state of the art performs guidance for the user rather than training the user's sensory interpretation skills, so it does not substantiate this task.

sources.system: Socially assistive robot for low vision rehabilitation (NCT04190134)
sources.title: Socially Assistive Robot for Low Vision Rehabilitation in Low Vision - Clinical Trials Registry
sources.claim: A socially assistive robot was trialled in low vision rehabilitation only as a motivational adjunct encouraging use of prescribed magnifiers; the robot delivers verbal encouragement and does not conduct hands-on tactile, kinesthetic or proprioceptive skill training.
sources.transferJustification: Nearest robotic system used inside vision rehabilitation practice; cited to show its role is motivational coaching on device use, not training clients to interpret non-visual sensory information, so it cannot complete this task.

sources.developer: University of Tsukuba / IBM Research collaborators (Tanaka, Takagi, Ochiai, Asakawa et al.)
sources.title: MotionBuddy: Exploring Tactile-Based Motion Learning with a Tabletop Humanoid Robot for Blind People (ACM/IEEE HRI 2026)
sources.claim: MotionBuddy is an exploratory tabletop humanoid used so blind participants can feel demonstrated body motions; it is a lab study with 11 participants, not an autonomous instructor delivering a full training session with assessment, correction and generalization.
sources.transferJustification: Most directly related demonstration: a robot conveying kinesthetic/tactile information to blind learners. Cited to show it is an exploratory prototype for motion demonstration only, without hands-on guidance, assessment or functional-context training, so it does not substantiate whole-instance completion.

sources.developer: University of Greifswald / BDH-Klinik Greifswald (Platz et al.)
sources.title: Analysis of the therapeutic interaction provided by a humanoid robot serving stroke survivors as a therapeutic assistant for arm rehabilitation
sources.claim: In the E-BRAiN system a humanoid robot acts as a therapeutic assistant for stroke arm rehabilitation in a clinic, but sessions still involve supervising staff/therapists and helpers who provide the physical assistance; the robot supplies information and feedback only.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robot-delivered sensorimotor rehabilitation training in a structured clinic. Cited to show that even in the most favourable structured setting, robot-assisted therapy still requires human staff for physical guidance and safety, so an unattended robot cannot deliver an equivalent training session.

tasks.label: Assess clients' functioning in areas such as vision, orientation and mobility skills, social and emotional issues, cognition, physical abilities, and personal goals.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Comprehensive functional low-vision evaluation in a vision rehabilitation clinic: interview the client about daily-living goals, present distance/near acuity charts, contrast sensitivity and visual-field screening materials, observe reading performance under varied lighting, trial magnifiers and CCTVs, note eccentric viewing, and write up findings into a rehabilitation plan.

Orientation and mobility assessment in the community: accompany the client along residential sidewalks, uncontrolled and signalized street crossings, and a bus stop; observe long-cane technique, drop-offs, traffic-sound judgment, route memory, gait and fatigue; intervene physically for safety; grade the client's independent travel skills.

In-home vision rehabilitation therapist assessment: visit a private residence, observe the client performing kitchen, grooming, medication-management and household tasks; evaluate lighting, glare, clutter and marking needs; interview client and family about emotional adjustment, cognition and personal goals.

School-based functional vision and learning-media assessment of a student with visual impairment: observe near and distance tasks in the classroom, travel in hallways, cafeteria and playground; present test targets and materials; consult with teachers; document functional implications for the IEP.

Facility-based assessment of a newly visually impaired patient at a hospital, VA blind rehabilitation center or nursing home: bedside/clinic evaluation of functional vision, cognition screening, balance and physical abilities, psychosocial adjustment, and goal setting with the care team.

sources.system: AI Suitcase (CAAMP / Miraikan / IBM Japan / OMRON et al.)
sources.developer: Consortium for Accessible AI-based Mobility Platform (Miraikan, IBM Japan, OMRON, Shimizu, Alps Alpine)
sources.title: Field Trials of Autonomous Navigation Robot for Visually Impaired People (CHI 2025 Extended Abstracts)
sources.claim: AI Suitcase is an autonomous suitcase-shaped navigation robot ... guides blind and low-vision people to destinations inside a science museum; it entered permanent daily operation at Miraikan in April 2024. It guides travelers but does not assess or grade a client's orientation and mobility skills.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: guiding a blind traveler through a public building. Cited to test transfer to O&M assessment; it does not transfer, because guiding requires no elicitation, scoring, or clinical judgment of the traveler's own cane technique, street-crossing judgment, or route learning, and it operates only on a pre-mapped institutional route.

sources.system: MoveCare / at-home socially assistive robot (Luperto et al.)
sources.developer: Università degli Studi di Milano and collaborators (EU MoveCare project)
sources.date: 2024-2025 (Int. J. Social Robotics 2024; Science Robotics focus 2025)
sources.title: Social robot for at-home cognitive monitoring | Science Robotics
sources.claim: A socially assistive mobile robot combined with IoT sensing operated autonomously in older adults' own homes for extended periods, administering cognitive stimulation and monitoring, without a human supervisor present. It covers a narrow cognitive-monitoring sub-step, not a functional vision or daily-living assessment.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated in-home cognitive monitoring of older adults. It addresses only the 'cognition' fragment of this assessment task and produces monitoring indicators, not a clinician-grade functional assessment of vision, mobility, physical ability and goals, so it does not substantiate whole-instance completion.

sources.title: Eyes on the future: Vision screening comes to self-service kiosks | Kiosk Marketplace
sources.claim: Eyebot self-service kiosks perform automated refraction and visual acuity measurement to generate an eyeglass prescription in minutes, piloted in Walmart Vision Centers and Sam's .... They measure refractive error only; optometric bodies note they are not a comprehensive eye exam, and they perform no functional-vision, mobility, cognitive or goal assessment.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated measurement of visual acuity and refraction. It does not transfer: a low-vision rehabilitation assessment measures functional use of residual vision under real task and lighting conditions, trials optical devices, and integrates psychosocial and mobility findings, none of which the kiosk performs.

tasks.label: Teach clients to travel independently, using a variety of actual or simulated travel situations or exercises.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Neighborhood outdoor cane-travel lesson: specialist accompanies a blind adult or student on residential sidewalks, physically demonstrating and correcting long-cane grip, arc and shorelining, teaching curb detection and traffic analysis, and staying close enough to physically block a step into the roadway or into a drop-off. Weather, parked cars, driveways and construction vary day to day.

Public transit / downtown business-district lesson: teaching bus or rail boarding, fare payment, locating stops, crossing complex signalized intersections with turning traffic, and recovering from disorientation in a crowded commercial area, with the instructor shadowing and intervening on safety.

Indoor route and familiarization lesson inside an institution (school, workplace, rehab agency, hospital): trailing walls, protective techniques, stairs, elevators, landmark/cue identification, learning routes to classroom, cafeteria or office, with the client wearing occluders and the instructor monitoring and physically prompting.

Simulated / controlled practice in an agency mobility lab or gym: pre-cane and human-guide technique with hand-over-hand instruction, obstacle courses set up by the instructor, blindfold simulation for low-vision clients, drills repeated with immediate corrective feedback before real-street work.

Home-based lesson with an older adult with low vision or a client with multiple disabilities: safe movement around furniture, stairs and thresholds, use of remaining vision and contrast, getting to the mailbox or a neighbor's door, adapting to an idiosyncratic, cluttered dwelling and family routines.

sources.developer: Miraikan / Carnegie Mellon University / CAAMP consortium (Alps Alpine, OMRON, Shimizu, Mitsubishi)
sources.title: Miraikan Accessibility Lab. | Miraikan - The National Museum of Emerging Science and Innovation
sources.claim: The AI Suitcase (CaBot lineage, Miraikan/CMU/CAAMP) is an autonomous navigation robot ... blind and visually impaired users to destinations while avoiding obstacles, running daily trial operations at Miraikan and field trials in malls, an airport and outdoor routes. It substitutes for the traveler's own navigation; it does not instruct, assess, or build the client's independent travel skills.
sources.transferJustification: Related task = robot-guided navigation for blind travelers in the same environments (facility corridors, malls, streets). Transfer to this task FAILS: the robot performs the travel for the user rather than teaching cane technique, route problem-solving or traffic analysis, and provides no demonstration, error correction, or competency assessment, so the accepted output of an O&M lesson (a client who can travel that route unaided) is not produced.

sources.developer: University of Greifswald / BDH-Klinik Greifswald and partners
sources.title: Technology Acceptance and Usability of a Therapy System with a Humanoid Robot Serving as Therapeutic Assistant for Post-Stroke Arm and Neurovisual Rehabilitation
sources.claim: E-BRAiN is a humanoid-robot therapy system that autonomously leads daily evidence-based rehabilitation sessions (arm basis/ability training, neglect therapy) for stroke survivors in a clinic room, adapting to individual assessments and progress. It is the closest demonstrated case of a robot delivering therapist-style training, but is confined to seated, tabletop exercises in a fixed clinical space.
sources.transferJustification: Related task = robot-delivered rehabilitation instruction to a patient. Transfer to O&M travel instruction FAILS: E-BRAiN is a stationary social robot coaching prescribed seated arm/visual exercises; it does not travel with a client, cannot demonstrate or hand-over-hand correct long-cane technique, cannot observe gait and cane arc while walking, and cannot supervise or physically intervene in safety-critical curb and street-crossing practice.

sources.title: Meet Glidance, the US startup reinventing assistive technology with Glide, the world's first self-guided mobility aid
sources.claim: Glide by Glidance is a self-guided (autonomous) mobility aid for blind and low-vision users, in beta with initial shipping to early customers announced for 2026. Like a guide robot, it steers the user around obstacles; it is a travel substitute, not an instructional system.
sources.transferJustification: Related task = autonomous guidance of a blind pedestrian. Transfer FAILS for the same reason as the AI Suitcase: the device replaces the traveler's wayfinding rather than teaching skills, and provides no lesson planning, technique demonstration, corrective feedback, or safety supervision of a learner practicing unaided travel.

tasks.label: Teach self-advocacy skills to clients.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

tasks.label: Provide consultation, support, or education to groups such as parents and teachers.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

tasks.label: Teach independent living skills or techniques, such as adaptive eating, medication management, diabetes management, and personal management.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: In-home instruction in adaptive eating and kitchen technique for an older adult with macular degeneration: therapist demonstrates plate-clock orientation, locating food, pouring with a liquid-level indicator, cutting and spreading, safe stovetop/microwave use; uses hand-under-hand modeling, applies tactile bump dots to dials, observes and corrects the client's technique in the client's own cluttered kitchen over several sessions.

In-home teaching of medication and diabetes management: sorting and tactile/large-print labeling of pill bottles, setting up a weekly organizer, teaching insulin measurement with a click-count syringe device or pen, non-visual use of a talking glucometer and lancet, foot-check routine; therapist physically demonstrates, guides the patient's hands, and verifies accurate doses.

In-home personal management instruction: grooming and shaving, clothing identification and coordination systems (tags, braille labels), money and mail identification, laundry, and household organization/cleaning routines; therapist demonstrates the technique with the client's own belongings and coaches practice trials.

Instruction in an agency or VA blind rehabilitation center's training kitchen/apartment or clinic ADL room: standardized adaptive equipment, controlled premises, one-on-one session teaching cooking, eating, and medication-organization techniques with graded practice and assessment.

Group class or school-based instruction at a controlled facility (agency low-vision program group cooking/personal-management class, or a school life-skills room for a student with visual impairment): multiple learners, demonstration to the group, then hands-on correction of each learner's technique.

sources.system: AI and robotic exercise coaches (post-stroke rehabilitation)
sources.developer: academic consortium (Int. J. Social Robotics study with therapists and post-stroke survivors)
sources.title: Enabling AI and Robotic Coaches for Physical Rehabilitation Therapy: Iterative Design and Evaluation with Therapists and Post-stroke Survivors
sources.claim: AI/robotic rehabilitation coaches that guide patients through therapy remain research prototypes; they coach verbally and by monitoring exercises, and their deployment in care is still described as a challenge.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robot-delivered rehabilitation coaching. It is the closest analogue to teaching rehabilitation skills, but the evidence shows only exercise monitoring and verbal encouragement at research stage, with no hands-on demonstration or technique correction, so it does not transfer to teaching adaptive eating, medication or diabetes management.

sources.title: NEO humanoid designed for household use, available for preorder
sources.claim: The most capable general-purpose home humanoid sold today handles only basic fetching/tidying autonomously and relies on scheduled human teleoperators for chores it does not know.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: general household manipulation in a private home, the setting of most instances of this task. Even for simple chores the system needs teleoperation, so it cannot perform the far harder hands-on demonstration and technique correction required here.

sources.system: UW Personal Robotics Lab robot-assisted feeding system
sources.developer: University of Washington Personal Robotics Lab
sources.title: Video: Assistive-feeding robot gets tested outside the lab
sources.claim: State-of-the-art assistive feeding robots substitute for a person's arm at mealtime for users with motor impairment, acquiring entrees with about 80% accuracy outside the lab; they do not teach non-visual eating technique.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robot manipulation of food at a table, the object domain of adaptive-eating instruction. It shows manipulation competence but performs the activity for the user rather than instructing a visually impaired learner, and its ~80% acquisition accuracy is below worker-quality teaching performance.

tasks.label: Monitor clients' progress to determine whether changes in rehabilitation plans are needed.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

tasks.label: Identify visual impairments related to basic life skills in areas such as self care, literacy, communication, health management, home management, and meal preparation.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

tasks.label: Design instructional programs to improve communication, using devices such as slates and styluses, braillers, keyboards, adaptive handwriting devices, talking book machines, digital books, and optical character readers (OCRs).

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

tasks.label: Train clients to use adaptive equipment, such as large print, reading stands, lamps, writing implements, software, and electronic devices.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Optical device training in a low-vision clinic or agency training room: therapist hands the client a prescribed handheld/stand magnifier or telescope, physically sets the correct eye-to-lens focal distance, guides the client's hand and head posture, positions reading material and a task lamp, watches technique and corrects it, and grades tasks from single words to continuous text until the client reads independently.

Electronic/video magnifier and computer training at an agency or clinic workstation: setting up a desktop CCTV, portable magnifier, tablet or PC with ZoomText/JAWS/VoiceOver; placing the client's hands on the X-Y table or keyboard, teaching control layout tactilely, adjusting contrast/magnification, loading documents, and coaching keystroke and tracking skills over repeated sessions.

In-home training on non-optical aids: reading stands, task lighting placement, bold-line paper, signature/writing guides, 20/20 pens, large-print labels, talking clocks and glucometers. Therapist works in the client's own furniture and lighting, repositions lamps and chairs, uses hand-under-hand guidance with an elderly or newly blind client, and adapts to clutter, pets and family members present.

Training at a school or workplace station: fitting a student's or employee's own desk with a video magnifier, monitor arm, screen-reader software or braille display; adjusting equipment to the existing workstation and training the person in the actual work routine, coordinating with teachers/employers.

Small group class or device demonstration at a rehabilitation agency or support group: therapist circulates among several clients at a table, distributes lamps, magnifiers and large-print materials, demonstrates each device, and individually corrects each participant's handling.

sources.developer: Universidad Carlos III de Madrid / research groups (SoftBank Robotics NAO platform)
sources.title: On the Use of Social Robots for Rehabilitation: The Case of NAO Physio
sources.claim: NAOTherapist is a robotic architecture in which a NAO social robot autonomously runs non-contact upper-limb rehabilitation sessions, demonstrating and monitoring exercises for patients; it is the closest robotic analog to a therapist-delivered training session, but it never handles equipment or physically guides a client's hands, and it is a research demonstration in clinical/lab settings rather than adaptive-device instruction for visually impaired clients.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robot-delivered rehabilitation coaching. Transfer fails for this task because the robot only speaks and gestures; it does not set focal distance of a magnifier, position lamps or reading stands, or provide the hand-under-hand tactile guidance that instruction of blind and low-vision clients requires.

sources.developer: SoftBank Robotics (deployed by clinical research groups)
sources.title: Empathic robots on future health care teams: Researchers review Pepper and NAO robot effectiveness
sources.claim: Pepper humanoid robots have been used ... assist rehabilitation exercises with patients (e.g., auditory rehabilitation for a child with a cochlear implant at home) as reviewed research/pilot use; the robot provides social engagement and exercise prompting only, with no manipulation of adaptive equipment and no evidence of autonomous end-to-end session delivery.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robot-supported sensory rehabilitation coaching. It does not substantiate this task because no equipment is handled by the robot, autonomy is not established, and the interaction is engagement/prompting rather than teaching a client to operate optical, lighting, writing, or electronic devices.

sources.system: Robot-assisted therapy platforms (PR2, JACO, NAO, Pepper, PARO; hand-therapy platforms)
sources.title: Robotics in Physical Rehabilitation: Systematic Review - PMC
sources.claim: Surveys of robotics in physical rehabilitation describe the state of the art as exoskeletons/end-effector motor trainers plus social robots (NAO, Pepper, PARO) used for engagement; no system is reported that instructs patients in the use of adaptive daily-living equipment, and robot-assisted therapy generally still requires a therapist to set up the patient and configure the equipment.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic rehabilitation therapy generally. Cited as a scope check: the reviewed field contains no system that trains a client to use low-vision adaptive equipment, supporting negative judgments rather than any positive one.

tasks.label: Participate in professional development activities, such as reading literature, continuing education, attending conferences, and collaborating with colleagues.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

tasks.label: Obtain, distribute, or maintain low vision devices.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Low vision clinic/rehab center: after the evaluation, the therapist pulls the recommended device (handheld or stand magnifier, spectacle-mounted telescope, filters, task lamp, portable electronic magnifier) from stock, sets it up for that patient (focal distance, magnification, frame/nosepad fit, battery install), verifies with the patient that it works for the target task, hands it over with case and instructions, and records the dispensing.

Agency/clinic office: obtaining devices - selecting vendors and models against a client's prescription and funding source (state agency, VA, insurance, donation), placing purchase orders or authorizations, tracking backorders, then receiving the shipment, checking contents against the packing list, entering items into the inventory system and shelving them.

Workroom bench maintenance of the demo/loaner pool of mixed devices: cleaning and sanitizing optics and housings between users, replacing batteries and bulbs, charging electronics, tightening screws and readjusting frames/clips, functional testing of video magnifiers and their monitors/cables, relabeling and re-shelving, and updating loan records.

A client reports a device fault (electronic magnifier won't charge, telescope out of focus, broken handle/clip, monitor no image). The therapist diagnoses it in the clinic or over the phone, performs a minor repair or arranges a warranty return to the manufacturer, and issues a substitute loaner in the meantime.

Delivery and setup in the client's own environment (private home, apartment, school classroom, workplace): unpacking and assembling a desktop video magnifier or CCTV, connecting it to a monitor and power, positioning it and task lighting on the client's own furniture, adjusting settings, and confirming the client can operate it.

Intra-facility distribution of stock: retrieving requested devices, batteries and accessories from the central supply room of a hospital eye clinic, VA blind rehabilitation center or agency, transporting them to the clinician, therapy room or patient room where they are needed, and logging the transaction.

sources.title: How Diligent's Robots Are Making a Difference in Texas Hospitals - IEEE Spectrum
sources.claim: Moxi, a mobile manipulator, autonomously picks supplies out of hospital supply closets and delivers them to patient rooms in commercial hospital deployments.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: fetch-and-deliver of small boxed clinical supplies inside a healthcare facility. Transfers to intra-facility distribution of low vision devices and accessories - comparable object size and weight, the same class of institution-controlled corridors and supply rooms, and no fine fitting precision required.

sources.title: Serve Robotics to Acquire Diligent Robotics, Expanding Physical AI Platform Beyond the Sidewalk
sources.claim: Moxi is in commercial deployment at scale: nearly 100 robots in over ... US hospital facilities, with more than 1.25 million autonomous ... completed.
sources.transferJustification: Establishes reliability and maturity of autonomous item transport in structured human work facilities, the environment relevant to intra-facility distribution of devices.

sources.title: Amazon opens its most automated facility - The Robot Report
sources.claim: Amazon's Sparrow robotic arm autonomously detects, selects and handles individual products across a very large catalog inside fulfillment centers, where totes are presented to the machine.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: piece-picking of heterogeneous small goods from presented totes in a purpose-built cell. Supports an E1 counterfactual for retrieving a specified stock item, but covers only picking - not clinical selection, patient fitting, or device servicing.

sources.title: KUKA Robots Used in Refurbishment of Electronics | KUKA Global
sources.claim: Assurant's device recovery operation uses 18 KUKA AGILUS robots in dedicated cells for cosmetic condition scanning and data collection/reset of pre-owned mobile devices - automated inspection of standardized electronics in a fixtured, purpose-built line.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated inspection/processing of consumer electronic devices. Cited for completeness - it handles a narrow set of standardized phone models with dedicated fixtures and performs no physical servicing (no lens cleaning, battery or bulb change, optical alignment, frame adjustment), so it does not transfer to bench maintenance of heterogeneous low vision aids.

tasks.label: Collaborate with specialists, such as rehabilitation counselors, speech pathologists, and occupational therapists, to provide client solutions.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

tasks.label: Refer clients to services, such as eye care, health care, rehabilitation, and counseling, to enhance visual and life functioning or when condition exceeds scope of practice.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

tasks.label: Administer tests and interpret test results to develop rehabilitation plans for clients.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Clinic-based comprehensive low vision evaluation in a low vision rehabilitation service: therapist seats and orients a visually impaired (often elderly) client, presents distance and near acuity charts at calibrated distances under controlled lighting, occludes eyes, runs contrast sensitivity (Pelli-Robson/Mars), confrontation or tangent-screen field screening, MNRead/continuous-text reading assessment, and trials a series of hand/stand magnifiers, telescopes and CCTV settings, then interprets results and writes a rehabilitation plan with magnification, lighting and training goals.

Home visit functional vision and ADL assessment by a vision rehabilitation therapist: in the client's own house or apartment (variable layout, pets, clutter, poor or glary lighting), the therapist has the client perform real tasks - pouring, stove-dial and medication identification, reading mail, marking appliances - measures illumination with a light meter, checks contrast and glare, watches for fall hazards, and writes a plan of home modifications, device recommendations and training objectives.

Community orientation and mobility assessment: specialist accompanies the client on residential sidewalks, a commercial block, bus stop and signalized/uncontrolled street crossings, evaluating long-cane technique, protective techniques, drop-offs, traffic alignment and judgment, sun glare and dusk performance, staying close enough to intervene physically for safety, then writes the O&M rehabilitation plan and route goals.

School-based assessment of a student with visual impairment: functional vision assessment and learning media assessment carried out in the classroom, hallways, cafeteria, stairwells and playground of a public school, including near/distance task performance, print size and lighting trials, and travel skills within the campus, feeding into IEP goals and a service plan.

Facility-based assessment in a residential blind rehabilitation center, rehab hospital, or skilled nursing facility: standardized intake battery on a frail or newly blinded patient at bedside or in a therapy room - functional vision screening, assistive technology and computer-access evaluation, ADL and indoor travel screening - interpreted into an individualized rehabilitation plan and documented in the medical record.

sources.title: A New Era of Autonomous Eye Care | EYOTO
sources.claim: Eyoto's Aetheia:Auto is a commercially deployed motorized digital slit lamp that autonomously aligns and performs anterior eye examination procedures in eye clinics without technician input; it produces images/measurements for clinician review, not a functional low-vision test battery or a rehabilitation plan.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated ophthalmic examination in a clinic. It shows a machine can autonomously position optics at a seated patient's eye, but it does not administer functional-vision tests (acuity charts, contrast, reading, magnifier trials), does not observe task performance, and does not produce a rehabilitation plan, so it does not substantiate completion of any instance of this task.

sources.system: Pepper humanoid robot for neuropsychological assessment
sources.developer: IRCCS Centro Neurolesi Bonino-Pulejo (Formica et al.)
sources.title: Humanoid robots for psychological assessment in mild cognitive impairment: from evaluation to the future of AI-driven data prediction systems
sources.claim: A humanoid robot (Pepper) was used in a clinical study to administer the MMSE cognitive test to patients with mild cognitive impairment, compared against neuropsychologist administration; the interaction is speech/tablet based with no handling of physical test materials.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robot-administered standardized clinical testing. It is the closest demonstration of a robot 'administering tests', but it is verbal/tablet screening in a research protocol with unclear autonomy, involves no calibrated presentation of optotypes, occlusion, magnifier trials or observation of a visually impaired client's task performance, and yields scores rather than a rehabilitation plan.

sources.title: Technology Acceptance and Usability of a Therapy System with a Humanoid Robot Serving as Therapeutic Assistant for Post-Stroke Arm and Neurovisual Rehabilitation
sources.claim: In the E-BRAiN robot-assisted neurorehabilitation system, the humanoid robot autonomously runs prescribed daily therapy sessions but the treatment plan is prescribed and personalised by a human therapist; the robot explicitly does not take therapeutic decisions.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robot-delivered rehabilitation therapy, including neurovisual rehabilitation. The most advanced fielded rehab robot still requires a human clinician to assess and set the plan, indicating the assessment-and-plan output of this task is not produced by robotic systems even in structured clinical settings.

sources.date: 2019 (ASSETS paper); guide-robot line of work continuing through 2026
sources.title: CaBot: Designing and Evaluating an Autonomous Navigation Robot for Blind People
sources.claim: Autonomous navigation robots for blind and low-vision travelers (e.g., the CaBot suitcase robot) guide users along routes, but they provide travel assistance rather than evaluating a client's travel skills or producing an O&M rehabilitation plan.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robots operating alongside blind travelers in the same environments where an O&M assessment occurs. Capability does not transfer: these systems substitute for the cane or guide, they do not score cane technique, traffic judgment or street-crossing performance, nor intervene as a sighted guide, so they cannot complete the assessment instance.

tasks.label: Train clients to read or write Braille.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Vision rehabilitation therapist teaches an older adult with recent vision loss (e.g., macular degeneration, diabetic retinopathy) uncontracted braille for labeling and note-taking, in the client's home or a rehab agency office: explaining the cell, assigning tactile discrimination drills, correcting reading technique verbally, assessing progress.

Therapist instructs a working-age blind client in contracted (UEB) literary braille over a series of sessions at a rehabilitation center classroom: presenting lessons, dictating for the client to write on a Perkins brailler or slate and stylus, checking written output for errors and giving corrective feedback.

Braille writing mechanics instruction: teaching correct use of the slate and stylus or Perkins brailler (paper insertion, key combinations, spacing, erasing), including demonstration and occasional hand positioning guidance during a face-to-face session.

Teaching braille via refreshable braille display / notetaker or braille-enabled computer and phone, in the client's home or workplace: explaining chords and commands, coaching the client through reading electronic braille, troubleshooting technique.

Remote or telerehabilitation braille instruction delivered by phone or video to a client who has materials mailed to them (distance-learning model), with the therapist explaining lessons, listening, and grading returned braille work.
