tasks.label: Provide emergency or other appropriate medical care to participants with symptoms or signs of physical distress.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Hospital-based outpatient cardiac or pulmonary rehab session: a monitored participant develops chest discomfort, dyspnea, lightheadedness, an arrhythmia on telemetry, or an abnormal blood-pressure response mid-exercise. The exercise physiologist stops the exercise, physically steadies the person and gets them into a chair, obtains manual BP, pulse, SpO2 and a rhythm strip, applies oxygen or gives sublingual nitroglycerin under standing orders, alerts the RN/physician, and stays with the patient until the episode resolves or EMS/rapid response arrives.

Clinical exercise testing lab (graded exercise/stress test): the patient meets test-termination criteria (ST changes, hypotensive response, ventricular ectopy, pallor, near-syncope). The physiologist stops the treadmill/ergometer, physically supports the patient off the moving belt to a chair or exam table, keeps electrodes and cuff in place for recovery BP/ECG, positions the patient supine with legs elevated if hypotensive, and summons the supervising physician.

Life-threatening event in the rehab gym or testing lab: a participant collapses, becomes unresponsive, or arrests. The physiologist activates the code, lowers the person to the floor, checks responsiveness/pulse/breathing, begins chest compressions, applies AED pads and delivers a shock, provides bag-valve-mask ventilation, and hands off to the code team.

Commercial fitness center, corporate wellness, or university/community exercise program: a client faints, becomes hypoglycemic, hyperventilates, overheats, or sustains a musculoskeletal injury (ankle sprain, muscle strain) during a session. The physiologist stops activity, guides or supports the person to sit or lie down, checks vitals and symptoms, applies ice/compression, gives fluids or glucose, and decides whether to call EMS, then documents the incident.

Off-premises setting: an outdoor group walking/exercise class in a park or on a track, a community health-fair fitness screening, or a home visit for home-based cardiac rehab. A participant becomes dizzy, short of breath, or falls on uneven ground; the physiologist must assess and provide first aid in an as-found space with no fixed layout, variable weather, and only a portable kit, then arrange transport or EMS.

sources.title: Swisslog Healthcare Partners with Diligent Robotics to Enhance Hospital Logistics
sources.claim: The most widely deployed healthcare robot fleet in US hospitals, Diligent Robotics' Moxi, performs autonomous point-to-point logistics (supply and pharmacy deliveries) in hospital corridors; it does not assess or physically treat patients.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: hospital material transport. It does NOT transfer to emergency care of a distressed exerciser — Moxi carries items between rooms and has no capability to assess symptoms, take vitals, support a collapsing person, or administer treatment. Cited to show the state of deployed hospital robotics.

sources.title: Eldercare robot helps people sit and stand, and catches them if they fall
sources.claim: The most advanced research robot for physically catching and lifting people who lose balance, MIT's E-BAR, is still remote-controlled rather than autonomous, and has only been tested in a lab mock-up of a home.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: physically supporting/catching a person who is losing balance, the closest robotic analogue to steadying a symptomatic exerciser. It cannot support a positive judgment because it is teleoperated and performs no assessment or medical care.

sources.developer: Everdrone / Karolinska Institutet, Region Västra Götaland
sources.title: Drone delivery of automated external defibrillators compared with ambulance arrival in real-life suspected out-of-hospital cardiac arrests: a prospective observational study in Sweden
sources.claim: Autonomous AED-carrying drones deployed in Sweden fly a defibrillator to suspected out-of-hospital cardiac arrests, but the device is applied and CPR performed by human bystanders and EMS.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: emergency response to cardiac arrest. Transfer fails — the robot only transports equipment to the scene; a human must open the case, place pads, deliver the shock and perform compressions, which is the physical care this task requires.

sources.developer: Stryker / Jolife (used by South Central Ambulance Service)
sources.title: Robot paramedic delivers CPR to heart attack patients
sources.claim: Mechanical CPR devices such as LUCAS deliver chest compressions, but they are carried, positioned on the patient and switched on by human paramedics after human assessment.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: delivering chest compressions during arrest. It cannot substantiate completion because the device is a human-applied appliance: humans recognise the arrest, expose the chest, place the piston and initiate it; the machine performs no assessment, airway, defibrillation or handover.

instances.label: Hospital-based cardiac/pulmonary rehab gym: orienting a post-MI, post-CABG or COPD patient to the exercise floor by physically demonstrating correct use of the treadmill (safety clip, handrails, speed/incline keys), recumbent/upright cycle ergometer (seat adjustment, workload), NuStep and arm ergometer, including target heart-rate/RPE stopping cues, while the telemetry-monitored patient watches and then repeats.

Wellness/fitness center or clinic weight room: demonstrating resistance training to a client — adjusting seat height and pin on selectorized machines, showing full range of motion, grip, breathing and tempo on chest press/lat pulldown, and performing reps with dumbbells, kettlebells or elastic bands, with spotting and setup cues.

Clinic, rehab gym or community senior center: personally performing a warm-up / stretching / range-of-motion / balance / light-calisthenic routine (arm raises, neck and trunk stretches, marching, sit-to-stands) for one client or a small seated group to imitate, with pacing and correction.

University or sports performance lab: demonstrating higher-skill movements to athletes or younger clients — barbell squat/deadlift technique, plyometric jumps and landings, agility ladder drills, mat-based core exercises — at full speed and with correct loaded biomechanics.

Home visit or worksite/community wellness setting taken as found: demonstrating the prescribed home exercise program in the client's living room or office using a dining chair, wall, stairs or a band, adapting the demonstration to the space and the person's limitations.

sources.claim: "Gymmy", a Poppy Torso humanoid coupled to an RGB-D camera, physically demonstrates a set of physical training exercises and gives real-time corrective feedback; it was tested with 26 older adults aged 65-84 in their home environments and was designed for independent operation without external guidance.

tasks.label: Conduct stress tests, using electrocardiograph (EKG) machines.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Hospital or outpatient cardiology exercise lab: symptom-limited treadmill exercise ECG (Bruce protocol) on an adult with suspected coronary disease. Worker consents the patient, preps skin (shaving chest hair, abrading, alcohol), places 10 electrodes at palpated anatomic landmarks on varied body habitus, secures lead wires and cable harness, cuffs the arm, records supine/standing/hyperventilation baselines, starts and advances the treadmill, takes exercise blood pressures by auscultation over treadmill noise, watches ST segments, rhythm, symptoms and gait, coaches the patient, terminates on criteria, steadies the patient off the belt, monitors recovery, removes electrodes and prints the report.

Stress echocardiography or nuclear myocardial perfusion study in a hospital imaging suite: same 10-electrode hookup and treadmill supervision, plus coordinating with sonographer/nuclear technologist, timing radiotracer injection or the peak-exercise image window, and physically moving a fatigued patient from the treadmill onto the imaging table within seconds without dislodging leads.

Cardiopulmonary exercise test (CPET/VO2max) in an exercise physiology, pulmonary or sports-performance lab: calibrate the metabolic cart, fit and leak-check a mouthpiece with nose clip or face mask on the subject's face, place 12-lead ECG electrodes under the harness, run a ramp protocol on cycle ergometer or treadmill, collect RPE by hand signals, take BP, and stop at volitional exhaustion while supporting the subject.

Cardiac rehabilitation / clinical exercise program entry or progress testing on deconditioned, elderly or post-MI patients with telemetry: hookup on frail or obese skin, low-level or modified protocol, patients holding handrails or using walkers, frequent BP, high risk of dizziness, unsteadiness or arrhythmia requiring hands-on guarding and immediate test termination.

Pharmacologic stress test (dobutamine or regadenoson) for a patient unable to exercise: place electrodes and monitor continuously while supine, obtain serial BP and ECGs during infusion, watch for chest pain, arrhythmia or adverse reaction, assist the nurse/physician, and monitor recovery.

Mobile or field-based exercise ECG testing: worksite/firefighter or public-safety physicals, athletic team screening at a training facility or track, or research testing away from a clinic, using portable ECG and treadmill/step equipment in a room or outdoor space taken as found.

sources.title: Performance, Safety, and Patient Experience of an Autonomous Robotic Phlebotomy Device: A Multicenter Trial (Clinical Chemistry)
sources.claim: The most advanced autonomous patient-contact robot in routine clinical use performs venipuncture only: it locates a vein by imaging and inserts a needle into an arm held in a fixture in outpatient phlebotomy departments. It performs no skin preparation, multi-site electrode placement, or supervision of an exercising patient.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous instrumented contact with a patient's body in a clinical facility. It marks the frontier of autonomous patient-contact robotics - one fixtured limb, one puncture site - and does not transfer to conducting an exercise EKG stress test, which requires skin prep, ten landmark-located electrodes on a moving torso, auscultated exercise blood pressures, real-time ischemia/arrhythmia judgment and hands-on guarding of a fatigued patient.

sources.system: Autonomous lightweight cable-driven ultrasound robot (Tsinghua University / Beijing Tsinghua Changgung Hospital)
sources.developer: Tsinghua University School of Biomedical Engineering
sources.title: Beyond hospital reach: Autonomous lightweight ultrasound robot for liver sonography (arXiv 2510.08106)
sources.claim: An autonomous ultrasound robot mounted on the abdomen acquires standard liver imaging planes on human patients in a hospital ultrasound department, demonstrating autonomous force-controlled sensor contact with a patient's trunk, but only for imaging - not electrode application or exercise test supervision.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous placement of a sensor against a patient's trunk with anatomical localization. tasks.label: Measure oxygen consumption or lung functioning, using spirometers.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Clinical cardiopulmonary exercise test (CPET) in a hospital or clinical exercise physiology lab: physiologist calibrates the metabolic cart (gas and 3-L volume syringe), preps the patient (skin prep, 12-lead ECG electrodes, BP cuff, pulse oximeter), fits a leak-free face mask with headgear and flow sensor, verifies seal, runs a ramp protocol on cycle/treadmill, coaches the patient, monitors ECG/BP/SpO2 for termination criteria, then breaks down, disinfects and produces the VO2/VE/VCO2 report.

Diagnostic/screening spirometry in a clinic, cardiac-pulmonary rehab program, or occupational-health room: attach bacterial filter and disposable mouthpiece, apply nose clip, position the seated patient, verbally and physically coach repeated maximal FVC maneuvers, reject unacceptable efforts and repeat until ATS/ERS acceptability and repeatability are met (sometimes pre/post bronchodilator), then clean equipment and record results.

Maximal VO2max test on a healthy athlete or research subject in a university human-performance lab: calibrate the metabolic system, fit a mouthpiece/nose clip or headgear-mounted mask and HR strap, run a graded maximal treadmill or cycle protocol, obtain RPE and finger-stick lactate, verbally push the subject to volitional exhaustion, confirm max criteria, and sanitize the breathing valve/mask afterward.

Metabolic testing in a fitness center, wellness suite, or corporate health room: resting metabolic rate measurement with a ventilated hood or mask on a reclined client, or a submaximal test with a portable metabolic analyzer (e.g., wearable unit and face mask), including client positioning, mask sizing and seal check, coaching to a steady state, and equipment turnaround between clients.

Field or off-site testing: portable metabolic analyzer / handheld spirometer used on a running track, sports field, worksite, community screening event, or home visit, with unknown layout, weather and ambient conditions, subject clothing and helmets, and no fixed lab setup — the physiologist calibrates on site, fits the harness/mask, and manages the test amid bystanders and interruptions.

sources.developer: Lifeline Robotics / University of Southern Denmark (Esben H. Østergaard, Thiusius R. Savarimuthu et al.)
sources.title: Autonomous swab robot for naso- and oropharyngeal COVID-19 screening | Scientific Reports
sources.claim: An autonomous force-controlled swab robot (SR-NOCS) collected naso-/oropharyngeal samples from 52 patients in clinical studies, showing a robot can autonomously bring an instrument to a cooperative person's face; it does not fit breathing interfaces, coach respiratory maneuvers, or judge test quality.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous instrument placement at a seated patient's face in a clinical station. It is the closest demonstrated capability to fitting a mouthpiece/nose clip, but it is a single scripted-path contact with the head in a rest, and provides no evidence of mask sealing, coaching a maximal forced-expiration or exercise ramp, or ATS/ERS quality acceptance, so it does not substantiate completing a spirometry or CPET instance.

sources.title: Vitestro Achieves CE Marking for Autonomous Blood Drawing Device
sources.claim: Vitestro's Aletta is a CE-marked autonomous robotic phlebotomy device drawing blood from patients in European hospitals and labs under one supervisor for multiple devices — an autonomous robotic clinical procedure on humans, but for venipuncture, not respiratory measurement.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: an autonomous robot performing a routine diagnostic procedure on a seated patient inside a structured clinical facility. It shows the environment tier is reachable for patient-contact robots in principle, but the object (a fixtured arm and needle) and the absence of any respiratory interface, effort coaching, or exercise supervision mean it does not transfer to measuring oxygen consumption or lung function.

sources.claim: A fully autonomous robotic ultrasound ... scanned the thyroid region of human participants without human assistance at near-clinician quality, demonstrating autonomous robotic contact with a live human body in a hospital imaging setting.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous robotic sensor placement on a passive human body with force control in a clinic. Spirometry and CPET instead require sealing a breathing interface, eliciting and coaching a maximal voluntary effort, and accepting/rejecting maneuvers against ATS/ERS criteria; no part of this system addresses those steps, so it cannot substantiate completion.

instances.label: Phase II/III cardiac rehabilitation group session in a hospital-based outpatient rehab gym: 8-12 high-risk patients; physiologist hooks up telemetry, takes resting/exercise/recovery blood pressure and heart rate, leads warm-up, sets and adjusts individual workloads on treadmills, bikes and arm ergometers, supervises a resistance circuit with spotting, watches for angina/arrhythmia/dizziness and leads cool-down, ready to respond to an emergency.

Medically supervised group exercise class for moderate-risk clients with chronic disease (pulmonary rehab, diabetes, obesity, cancer survivorship, post-orthopedic) in a clinic or medical fitness center: oxygen saturation and RPE checks, oxygen tank management, individualized modifications for each participant, hands-on form correction and guarding during standing and resistance work.

Seated/chair-based strength, flexibility and circulation class for low-risk older or deconditioned participants at a senior center, hospital wellness center or assisted-living activity room: 10-25 participants follow a demonstrated routine to music, use light bands and dumbbells, receive verbal cueing and encouragement; leader watches for dizziness and hands out equipment.

General adult group conditioning class for low-risk clients at a corporate, community or university fitness center: full-body circuit, aerobic and strength/flexibility work on mats, benches and machines; leader demonstrates each movement, cues tempo, corrects form across the room, spots heavy lifts, adjusts equipment and scales intensity for individuals.

Group class held at a nonstandard venue taken as found - park boot camp, worksite break room floor, church or community hall - with variable layout, weather and footing, no fixed equipment and no institution keeping the space to a standard; leader adapts the session and the demonstrations to whatever space and surfaces are available.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: University or hospital exercise physiology lab, before a VO2max/CPET session: physiologist calibrates the metabolic cart — opens the certified calibration-gas cylinder and runs the two-point O2/CO2 analyzer calibration, then performs volume/flow calibration by stroking a 3-L syringe through the flow sensor at several flow rates, checks for leaks and drift, and logs results before the subject arrives.

Cycle or arm-crank ergometer calibration in a performance lab or cardiac rehab gym: zeroing the pendulum and checking belt/basket on a mechanically braked Monark with known hanging weights, or the periodic dynamic torque/power verification of an electronically braked ergometer across the workload and cadence range, adjusting settings and filing a calibration record.

Treadmill calibration in an exercise testing lab or fitness facility: marking the belt and counting revolutions over a timed interval (or using a tachometer) to verify displayed speed, checking grade/elevation with an inclinometer, adjusting controller constants or calling service, and documenting the check.

Clinical exercise/cardiac rehab setting: pre-test verification of the stress ECG system, sphygmomanometers/automated BP units, pulse oximeters, and daily 3-L syringe verification of the spirometer, with QC logged and out-of-tolerance units tagged before patients are tested.

Calibration/verification of weighing equipment: placing certified test masses on the clinic or lab scale and the hydrostatic-weighing balance, checking zero, linearity and span, adjusting or re-spanning the device, and recording the results.

Other body-composition and field-test equipment: BOD POD two-point volume calibration with the calibration cylinder, skinfold caliper jaw-gap and jaw-pressure checks against calibration blocks, DXA daily phantom QC, and lactate analyzer QC with standard solutions.

sources.date: product in commercial use; cited in peer-reviewed testing 2021-2024
sources.title: Metabolic Calibrator/Simulator - VacuMed
sources.claim: A commercial motor-driven calibration syringe/metabolic calibrator mechanically strokes air through a metabolic system's flow sensor at set volumes and rates and produces simulated VO2/VCO2 to verify and calibrate the whole metabolic measurement system.
sources.transferJustification: The volume/flow calibration step of a metabolic cart is exactly the syringe-stroke operation this machine performs mechanically, on the same flow sensors and connectors the physiologist uses.

tasks.label: Supervise maintenance of exercise or exercise testing equipment.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Hospital / outpatient cardiac-pulmonary rehab gym: routine (daily-weekly) equipment check round on treadmills, recumbent steppers, arm and cycle ergometers — start each unit and verify speed/incline/resistance and console readout, check safety lanyard clips, straps, handrails and fasteners, wipe down contact surfaces, sign the maintenance log and tag out anything faulty. Machines are in place on the rehab floor among patients and staff.

Clinical exercise testing lab (CPET/stress testing): pre-test quality control and calibration round — connect calibration gas and run gas analyzer calibration on the metabolic cart, attach the 3-L syringe to the flow sensor and perform strokes at several flow rates, verify treadmill speed/grade or ergometer power, check ECG cables/electrodes and the sphygmomanometer/BP device, judge results against tolerance, repeat or service if out of range, and record the QC in the lab log.

Fitness / wellness or corporate fitness center: scheduled preventive maintenance on selectorized and cable strength machines and cardio units — lubricate guide rods and chains, torque-check fasteners, inspect cables, pulleys, pins, belts and upholstery, replace frayed cables and worn treadmill belts, wax/inspect decks, and re-set the equipment for member use.

Breakdown response and outside-service coordination: a machine fails or a member/patient reports a fault; the physiologist reproduces and diagnoses the problem, tags the unit out of service, opens a work order with the biomed department or the equipment vendor, is present to oversee/verify the technician's repair, functionally tests the unit, returns it to service and updates the asset/warranty records.

Program-level supervision: writing and revising the preventive-maintenance schedule, training and assigning aides, students or techs to daily cleaning/inspection duties, auditing their logs and spot-checking equipment condition, ordering parts and cleaning supplies, and assembling maintenance/calibration documentation for accreditation or safety inspections.

sources.transferJustification: Related task: routine equipment inspection rounds with automatic logging. Same purpose as an equipment check round, but limited to standoff sensing on a fixed route; it establishes what deployed inspection robots do and do not do in an E2 facility.

tasks.label: Perform routine laboratory tests of blood samples for cholesterol level or glucose tolerance.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Point-of-care fingerstick lipid screen for a client in a clinic, cardiac-rehab or corporate-wellness exercise physiology room: verify fasting status, prep and lance the fingertip, collect ~35 uL into a capillary tube, load the cassette into a desktop analyzer (e.g., Cholestech LDX), run/record QC, read total cholesterol-HDL-LDL-triglycerides, log the result and discuss it with the client, dispose of sharps.

Venous sample in a hospital or university clinical exercise physiology lab: tourniquet and antecubital venipuncture into labeled vacutainer tubes, invert/hold clotting time, centrifuge, aliquot serum/plasma, run lipid panel and glucose on a bench clinical chemistry analyzer with calibration and QC, verify and document results in the client record.

Oral glucose tolerance test in a clinical exercise physiology lab: fasting baseline sample and reading, hand the client a 75 g glucose beverage and time its consumption, take timed capillary or venous samples at 30/60/120 minutes, watch the client for nausea, sweating or hypoglycemia, analyze each sample and plot the tolerance curve.

Blood sampling and immediate analysis around a graded exercise test: capillary glucose (and lactate) checks on a client on a treadmill or cycle ergometer or immediately post-stage, wiping sweat, steadying the moving hand or earlobe, applying the drop to the meter/analyzer at fixed workload intervals while simultaneously monitoring the client.

Off-site community or worksite health-fair screening: portable analyzer, folding table and supplies set up in a gym, church hall, employer break room or mobile van; fingerstick cholesterol and glucose for a queue of walk-in participants of varied age and skin condition, results recorded on forms and briefly counseled, sharps and biohazard waste packed out.

tasks.label: Measure amount of body fat, using such equipment as hydrostatic scale, skinfold calipers, or tape measures.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Skinfold caliper assessment (3- or 7-site Jackson-Pollock protocol) of a client at a health club, corporate fitness center, or community wellness center: the physiologist palpates bony landmarks, pinches and lifts a skinfold with thumb and forefinger, applies calipers 1 cm below the pinch, reads to 0.5 mm, repeats each site 2-3 times on a lightly clothed, standing/seated live client of highly variable body habitus, then computes body-fat percent and explains the result.

Tape-measure girth assessment (waist at iliac crest, hip, neck, arm, thigh) in a clinic exam room, cardiac-rehab gym, or fitness facility: the physiologist locates landmarks by palpation, wraps a flexible/spring-tension tape snugly without compressing tissue, keeps it level around the torso, reads to 0.1 cm, repeats for agreement, and applies circumference-based body-fat equations or waist-to-hip ratio.

Reference-method lab test in a university human-performance lab or hospital exercise-physiology lab: hydrostatic (underwater) weighing or air-displacement plethysmography — calibrating the tank/chamber, weighing and seating the participant, coaching maximal exhalation and full submersion over repeated trials or estimating thoracic gas volume, tare-weighting the chair, reading the scale, and computing body density and percent fat.

Device-assisted body-composition session in a clinical or wellness facility: prepping and operating a BIA analyzer, 3D optical scanner, or similar instrument (electrode/skin prep, bare feet and hands on contacts, posture and hydration protocol checks), then confirming with a tape or skinfold measurement and recording results in the client's chart.

Off-site screening with portable equipment: worksite health fair in a conference room or lobby, community event tent, team training room, or a home visit — calipers, tape, and a portable scale used in a found space with uncontrolled lighting, no fixed station, queues of participants, and varied clothing and body types.

sources.title: Equinox Locations Add Aescape, a Fully Automated Massage Bed - Athletech News
sources.claim: Aescape is a commercially deployed, fully automated robotic massage table with two force-controlled arms that 3D-scans a client's body and works on it autonomously inside fitness-club spas (Equinox). It is the closest deployed human-contact robot in a fitness facility, but it delivers massage strokes, not anthropometric measurement.
sources.transferJustification: Related task = robotic soft-tissue contact on a live human in an E2 fitness facility. Transfer FAILS for this task: Aescape applies broad compressive strokes to the back and legs; it does not palpate bony landmarks, grasp and lift a skinfold between two contacts, place calipers to 0.5 mm, wrap a tension tape around a torso, or output any body-composition value, so it cannot deliver the measurement the employer accepts.

sources.system: VxWave robotic tomographic ultrasound imaging system
sources.title: Vexev robotic ultrasound study meets endpoints - MassDevice
sources.claim: The most advanced deployed robot that takes physical measurements on live human bodies in a clinic is a semi-autonomous robotic ultrasound scanner limited to upper-limb vascular mapping; it still requires clinician involvement and produces vascular models, not body-fat estimates.
sources.transferJustification: Related task = robot-held probe contacting a patient's limb under force control in an E2 clinic. Transfer FAILS: the system is explicitly semi-autonomous, is confined to a single fixtured limb and a vascular imaging output, and no reported use measures subcutaneous fat at standardized sites or yields a percent-body-fat result.

sources.system: auto-RUSS (autonomous robotic ultrasound scanning system, 7-DOF arm)
sources.developer: Lin et al., academic group (Frontiers in Robotics and AI)
sources.title: Autonomous robotic ultrasound scanning system: a key to enhancing image analysis reproducibility and observer consistency in ultrasound imaging - PMC
sources.claim: Fully autonomous robotic ultrasound scanning with force control and visual servoing has been demonstrated only on phantoms in a laboratory comparison against physicians, not on live clients in a working facility.
sources.transferJustification: Related task = autonomous robotic contact measurement on tissue. Transfer FAILS: validation is on rigid tissue phantoms in a lab, not on compliant, breathing, differently shaped live clients, and the output is image reproducibility rather than a body-fat assessment.

sources.title: Clinically applicable optical imaging technology for body size and shape analysis: comparison of systems differing in design - PMC
sources.claim: Automated anthropometry in fitness and clinical settings is done by optical 3D body scanners (Styku, Fit3D): a depth camera images the client while a platform rotates them, producing circumferences and body-fat estimates. These are sensing instruments rather than robotic manipulators, and staff still position and instruct the client.
sources.transferJustification: Related task = automated circumference/body-composition measurement. It does not qualify as a robotic system under the definition used here: it is a camera plus a turntable that senses rather than a machine that manipulates the tape, calipers, or client, so it cannot substantiate robotic completion of the instance.

tasks.label: Conduct art therapy sessions, providing guided self-expression experiences to help clients recover from, or cope with, cognitive, emotional, or physical impairments.

instances.label: Individual outpatient art therapy session in a clinic or private practice studio: therapist offers a directive (e.g., draw a safe place), sits with an adult client coping with anxiety, depression or trauma, observes the process, attunes to affect, and leads verbal reflection on the imagery. Core work is relational, interpretive and verbal; art materials are used by the client.

Group art therapy session on an inpatient psychiatric or behavioral-health unit: therapist frames the theme, manages group dynamics and safety (including sharps/materials risk), supports 6-10 participants of varying acuity, and facilitates sharing and closure.

Bedside or rehab-gym session in a hospital, rehab facility or long-term care setting with a client recovering from stroke, TBI, cancer treatment or dementia: therapist adapts the directive and tools to motor and cognitive limits, may steady materials or offer hand-over-hand support, and grades the task to the client's tolerance.

School- or community-agency-based session with children or adolescents (special education, grief or trauma programs): therapist introduces a developmentally appropriate art task, maintains behavioral structure, and interprets play/art content for the treatment team.

Telehealth art therapy session by video: therapist guides the client through an art-making prompt with materials the client already has at home, watches the process on camera, and processes the resulting image verbally.

tasks.label: Select or prepare artistic media or related equipment or devices to accomplish therapy session objectives.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Group session prep in a clinic/hospital art therapy room: per the session plan, gather and lay out media for 6-12 participants — paper, brushes, tempera/acrylic in palettes or cups, water containers, glue, scissors, magazines, table coverings and smocks — one station per participant, then restock after.

Individual session media selection: from the studio cabinet the therapist picks a specific set of media matched to the client's goals and capacities (e.g., resistive pencils/collage for a client needing containment vs. fluid paint or clay for expression), assembles them on the table, and often stages a second option to swap in.

Specialized preparation of media and equipment: wedging and slicing clay, mixing paint/plaster/glazes, cutting mat board and tearing paper to size, stretching canvas, loading and firing a kiln, threading a loom or sewing machine, setting up cameras, tablets and drawing apps and charging devices.

Bedside/portable medical work: assemble an infection-control-compliant portable kit, wheel a supply cart to the patient room, and set materials up on an overbed table around IV lines and the patient's position, fitting adaptive aids (built-up grips, non-slip mats, tabletop easel) to the patient's physical or cognitive limits.

Off-site/community work: school multipurpose room, nursing-home dayroom, shelter, or a client's home — pack and transport supplies, screen materials against site safety rules (no sharps/solvents), and set up on whatever tables, floor space and lighting are found there.

sources.title: RightHand Robotics | Integrations and Workflows
sources.claim: RightHand Robotics' RightPick system autonomously picks a wide range of small consumer items from mixed-SKU totes and places them into designated cubbies to build kits/orders, in commercially deployed fixtured picking cells.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic kitting/order picking. Assembling a per-session set of art supplies from bins of pencils, tubes, brushes and packaged materials is the same act — identify specified small items and place them into a designated tray — at comparable precision and with the goods presented in totes as a purpose-built cell would present them.

sources.title: Amazon robotics: Meet the robots inside fulfillment centers
sources.claim: Amazon's Sparrow robotic arm, deployed in fulfillment centers, autonomously detects, selects and moves individual diverse products from containers into specific order totes.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: item selection from stock into an order tote. Selecting the named media for a session from stocked bins is the same identify-grasp-place operation over a comparably diverse catalogue of small consumer goods.

sources.title: Canvas, Camera, Brush, and Algorithms Enable Robot Artist's Beautiful Paintings
sources.claim: The e-David painting robot autonomously handles art media in a purpose-built rig: it selects among five brushes, dips them into a 24-colour paint repository, rinses them, and uses visual feedback to adjust.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic painting. It demonstrates machine handling of the exact media of this task — brushes, wet paint pots, rinse water — including tool changeover and cleaning, in a fixtured bench setup, which is what 'preparing artistic media' requires at E1.

sources.title: Automated Production Line in Ceramic Manufacturing | KUKA Global
sources.claim: At GSI Ceramica, KUKA robots autonomously move ceramic parts through processing stages and load them for firing in a 1,250 °C tunnel kiln on a production line.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: ceramic material handling and kiln loading. The art therapist's clay/kiln preparation involves the same materials and the same handling and firing steps, done here reliably in a fixtured production cell.

sources.title: Figure AI humanoids sort 28,000 packages in 24-hour autonomous test
sources.claim: Figure's Helix-02 humanoids ran multi-hour fully autonomous shifts in a logistics facility, picking packages and placing them onto conveyors using onboard perception, handling tens of thousands of items.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: sustained autonomous item handling at a conveyor-fed station. It shows current general-purpose manipulators can run long unattended shifts of varied-object pick-and-place when the work is presented to them, the E1 condition for material preparation.

sources.title: Diligent Robotics hits 1M picks with Moxi robot in healthcare settings - The Robot Report
sources.claim: Diligent Robotics' Moxi is deployed in US hospitals and autonomously delivers supplies, lab specimens and medications between locations; its deployed role is transport, not assembling or laying out task materials at a work surface.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: hospital supply logistics. It bounds what autonomous systems do inside E2 healthcare facilities today — point-to-point fetch and delivery — with no evidence of setting media out at a bedside or therapy table.

sources.title: Physical Intelligence's π0.5 VLA with Open-World Generalization
sources.claim: Physical Intelligence's pi-0.5 model was shown performing multi-step tidying chores in three real, previously unseen homes, but as a research demonstration rather than a reliability-qualified deployment.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: household object manipulation in unseen homes. It is the closest evidence for E3 material handling, but the demonstrated chores are coarse tidying at research success rates, not the reliable, precise setup of art media a client session requires.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Group art therapy session on an inpatient behavioral health unit or partial hospitalization program: the therapist introduces the day's directive to 6-10 adult clients, explains and demonstrates how to use the media (mixing acrylics, loading a brush, applying pastel), and gives ongoing verbal coaching as clients work at tables in a dayroom.

Individual outpatient session in a clinic or private practice office: the therapist offers a choice of media, explains and briefly demonstrates a technique (wedging and pinching clay, wet-on-wet watercolor), and adjusts the instruction verbally to the client's comfort, skill level, and therapeutic goals.

School- or agency-based children's group: the therapist gives step-by-step spoken and demonstrated directions for a yarn weaving, collage, or tempera project to 5-15 children, restating rules for safe media use and re-explaining steps to individual students who are stuck.

Older-adult or rehabilitation setting (skilled nursing facility, memory-care activity room, hospital bedside): the therapist instructs clients with cognitive or motor limitations, using simplified cueing, repeated demonstration, and sometimes hand-over-hand prompting for grip on a brush or clay tool.

Community program or telehealth group: the therapist instructs participants in a community center, shelter, or over video in the use of pre-supplied media kits (markers, air-dry clay, yarn), conveying technique by spoken explanation and on-camera or in-room demonstration.

tasks.label: Photograph or videotape client artwork for inclusion in client records or for promotional purposes.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Outpatient clinic / community mental-health art therapy studio: at the end of a session the therapist photographs a client's flat 2D piece (drawing, painting on paper, collage, pages of an art journal) on the worktable or against a wall with a phone or tablet, checking for glare, shadow and full-frame coverage, then uploads the image into the client's chart/EHR with correct client and date identifiers.

Clinic or hospital art studio: photographing a 3D piece (clay sculpture, mask, altered book, assemblage, shadow box) from several angles, sometimes while still fragile or drying, to document it before the client takes it home; images filed to the clinical record.

Inpatient bedside, psychiatric unit dayroom, or school classroom: photographing artwork where it was made, amid clutter, variable lighting and other people present, sometimes with the client holding the piece up; quick capture between sessions, filed to the record.

Promotional/exhibition work: staging and photographing (or shooting short video of) selected, consented, de-identified client pieces against a neutral background with attention to lighting and color fidelity for agency newsletters, exhibit catalogs, grant reports or social media.

Community or home-based practice: photographing artwork during a home visit, in a nursing-home resident's room, shelter, or hospice, with no dedicated space, uncontrolled lighting and furniture taken as found.

Large, immovable or ephemeral work: a group mural on a wall, a floor installation, a sand-tray arrangement, or an environmental piece that must be photographed or videotaped in place, one time only, before it is dismantled.

sources.title: Fraunhofer IGD develops automated robotic arm to scan cultural objects in 3D, now cooperating with Phase One
sources.claim: CultArm3D is a robot arm carrying a Phase One camera that autonomously plans viewpoints and captures color-faithful, high-resolution imagery of cultural objects placed on its turntable, producing archival-quality documentation of 3D artifacts.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: museum object digitization. Objects (sculptures, ceramics, mixed-media artifacts) are the same class and fragility as client 3D artwork, the imaging quality standard is higher than a clinical record photo, and the machine handles all camera positioning and capture once the object is presented.

sources.title: Fraunhofer IGD develops new and improved CultArm3D archival scanner
sources.claim: An earlier generation of the CultArm3D scanner is installed and in use at a museum, showing the imaging station is a real deployed device rather than a lab prototype.
sources.transferJustification: Same related task as above (object digitization); this item establishes deployment of the imaging station in a real institution.

sources.title: Software Technology - Ortery Product Photography
sources.claim: Ortery sells computer-controlled photography benches and camera-positioning robots in which software drives lights, turntable and camera to capture stills, 360 views and video of an object placed inside the enclosure, including flat-lay benches for flat items.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: product photography. The object handled (a flat sheet or a small 3D piece placed on the bench) and the required output (a well-lit, in-focus, correctly framed still or video for a record or catalog) match photographing client artwork; the machine performs framing, lighting and capture unattended.

sources.title: Automated Product Photography | Orbitvu Product Photo Booths
sources.claim: Orbitvu automated photo studios combine a motorized turntable, automated camera stand and LED lighting under software control to produce repeatable stills, video and 360-degree imagery of items placed in the booth.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated studio photography and video of objects. Establishes that both the photograph and the videotape variants of the task can be produced to publication (promotional) quality by a machine once the piece is placed in the station.

sources.developer: Treventus Mechatronics (installed at University of Tulsa McFarlin Library)
sources.title: McFarlin's new ScanRobot protects rare books while increasing access for students, scholars
sources.claim: The Treventus ScanRobot 2.0 MDS automatically turns pages and images bound paper originals at up to 2,500 pages per ..., and is installed and running in a university library where scanned images are automatically packaged for deposit.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated imaging of flat paper originals, including page handling of fragile material. This is the same object class and precision as photographing drawings, paintings on paper and multi-page art journals, and the machine both manipulates the paper and captures the image.

sources.title: Google Art Camera uses robotic system to take gigapixel photos of museum paintings
sources.claim: Google's Art Camera is a purpose-built robotic camera that, once an operator calibrates it to the edges of a ..., automatically shoots hundreds of focused close-ups of the artwork in museums, using laser and sonar focusing, to build gigapixel images.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: photographing two-dimensional artwork for a collection record. Same object (a painting or work on paper) and a far higher precision standard than a clinical record photo; the per-artwork operator calibration is equivalent to presenting/fixturing the work, which an E1 setting supplies.

sources.title: Automated Inspections Made Simple | Boston Dynamics
sources.claim: Boston Dynamics' Spot runs scheduled, unsupervised inspection missions inside industrial plants, walking a recorded route to fixed assets and capturing the same image from the same angle each time, with data uploaded to the Orbit platform.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous in-situ image capture of assets in a human work facility. It shows what mobile image capture can do today — repeat a human-taught route to fixed, known assets — which does not cover one-off framing of a newly made artwork whose location and appearance change every session.

roles.title: Music Therapists
roles.description: Plan, organize, direct, or assess clinical and evidenced-based music therapy interventions to positively influence individuals' physical, psychological, cognitive, or behavioral status.

tasks.label: Design or provide music therapy experiences to address client needs, such as using music for self-care, adjusting to life changes, improving cognitive functioning, raising self-esteem, communicating, or controlling impulses.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Group session in a skilled nursing facility or memory-care unit: therapist plans and leads familiar-song singing, rhythmic instrument play, and reminiscence to support cognition, mood, and social engagement for 6-12 older adults with dementia.

Individual bedside session in a hospital (oncology, ICU, palliative, or pediatric unit): therapist selects and performs live preferred music, uses entrainment/relaxation and verbal processing to address anxiety, pain perception, coping with life changes, and self-expression.

School or early-intervention session for children with autism or developmental delay: therapist designs music experiences (turn-taking songs, instrument choices, movement) targeting communication, attention, and impulse control, coordinated with IEP goals.

Behavioral-health or substance-use group in a psychiatric unit or outpatient clinic: therapist facilitates lyric analysis, songwriting, and drumming to build self-esteem, emotion regulation, and self-care skills, then documents progress toward treatment goals.

Planning and design work away from the client: reviewing assessments and referrals, writing individualized music therapy treatment plans and session protocols, preparing song lists/adaptations, and documenting outcomes in the chart.

Session delivered in a private home or via telehealth (hospice home visit, early-intervention home visit, remote outpatient session): therapist adapts receptive listening, singing, and caregiver-supported music use to the client's own environment.

tasks.label: Design music therapy experiences, using various musical elements to meet client's goals or objectives.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Board-certified music therapist in a skilled nursing / memory-care unit designs a weekly group session plan for residents with dementia: selects era-appropriate song repertoire, sets tempos and keys within the residents' vocal range, sequences familiar-song singing, rhythmic instrument play, and a closing relaxation piece, and maps each musical element to reminiscence, orientation, and agitation-reduction goals. Output is a written/mentally-held session design plus documentation linking elements to care-plan goals.

Pediatric hospital music therapist designs individualized experiences for a child facing a painful procedure or long admission: chooses preferred songs, decides between live entrained guitar/voice for procedural support versus active instrument play, sets tempo relative to the child's respiration, and plans adaptations for IV lines, isolation precautions, and fluctuating alertness, with goals of pain distraction and coping.

School-based music therapist designs experiences targeting IEP goals for students with autism or developmental disabilities: writes or adapts greeting/transition songs, structures call-and-response and fill-in-the-blank melodic prompts for expressive language, chooses adapted instruments and rhythmic cueing for motor and turn-taking goals, and aligns each experience with measurable objectives for the IEP team.

Behavioral/mental-health music therapist in an inpatient psychiatric or substance-use program designs lyric-analysis, songwriting, and drum-circle experiences for an adolescent or adult group: selects songs whose lyrics and harmonic character fit the group's themes, sequences improvisation rules and processing questions, and plans safety-conscious adaptations for acute symptoms, targeting emotional identification and coping-skill goals.

Neurologic rehabilitation music therapist designs standardized-technique protocols (rhythmic auditory stimulation for gait, melodic intonation therapy for aphasia, therapeutic instrumental music performance for upper-limb range of motion) for a stroke or TBI patient: computes cueing tempo from baseline cadence, plans progression increments, selects accent patterns and instrument placement, and coordinates the design with PT/OT/SLP goals.

tasks.label: Sing or play musical instruments, such as keyboard, guitar, or percussion instruments.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Group music session in a skilled nursing / memory care activity room: the therapist sits with 8-15 residents, plays acoustic guitar and sings familiar songs from a large repertoire, transposing keys to aging voices, slowing or driving tempo to the group's participation, substituting lyrics, and cueing residents holding hand drums, shakers and bells while watching for agitation, fatigue and respiratory cues.

Individual bedside session in a hospital or inpatient rehab unit (oncology, ICU, palliative care, NICU, stroke/neuro-rehab): the therapist brings a guitar, small keyboard or hand percussion to the room, plays and sings live at low volume, entrains tempo and dynamics to the patient's breathing, heart rate or gait cadence, takes song requests, and shifts or stops the music in response to clinical events, working around lines, monitors and family.

Individual pediatric session in a clinic or school therapy room: one child (often autistic or developmentally delayed) at a table or on the floor with the therapist, who plays a xylophone/keyboard/drum, models short patterns, waits for and reinforces the child's turn-taking imitation on the instrument, and adjusts pattern and tempo to the child's response.

Group session in a special education classroom or pediatric day program: the therapist plays guitar or keyboard and sings hello/goodbye and target songs while circulating to hand out and collect drums, egg shakers and tone bars among 5-10 children, adapting the music live to behavior, sensory needs and adaptive positioning.

Group session on an inpatient psychiatric unit or in a behavioral health clinic: the therapist accompanies on guitar or keyboard for lyric analysis, group songwriting and drum-circle improvisation with adolescents or adults, improvising under clients' irregular playing and singing, and changing style or ending abruptly if content escalates.

Home-based hospice or in-home pediatric session in a private residence: the therapist carries a guitar into an unmodified living room or bedroom, sets up beside a bed or recliner amid furniture, pets, oxygen equipment and family members, and sings and plays live for client and family, often ending with a legacy song or recording.

sources.system: NAO robot music-therapy platform (autonomous xylophone-playing intervention)
sources.developer: Academic research team, published in Frontiers in Robotics and AI
sources.title: A Music-Therapy Robotic Platform for Children With Autism: A Pilot Study
sources.claim: A fully autonomous NAO-based music-therapy platform localized and struck a xylophone with its arms, played customized songs, listened to and scored the child's played imitation and gave feedback, across 50 turn-taking intervention sessions with 9 autistic and 7 typically developing children in a dedicated instrumented experiment room.

sources.developer: Georgia Tech Center for Music Technology (Gil Weinberg)
sources.title: Interactive improvisation with a robotic marimba player (Autonomous Robots)
sources.claim: Shimon, a robotic marimba player, listens to a live human musician and autonomously improvises percussion accompaniment in real time, performing on stage with human players.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: live robotic musicianship. It shows a machine physically playing a percussion instrument and adapting to a human in real time, the closest analogue to a therapist's live playing, but demonstrated with trained musicians in concert/lab performance, not with patients in a clinical session.

sources.system: Human-robot cooperative piano playing system (cobot pianist with RNN improvisation and adaptive controller)
sources.title: Human-Robot Cooperative Piano Playing with Learning-Based Real-Time Music Accompaniment
sources.claim: A collaborative robot arm plays a physical piano and generates real-time chord accompaniment synchronized to a human performer's melodic input, validated in laboratory experiments.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: keyboard accompaniment of a live human. Shows autonomous physical keyboard playing with tempo adaptation on a fixed instrument in a lab rig; it does not sing, transpose repertoire for clients, or respond to clinical cues.

sources.title: UC Davis launches first long-term U.S. study led by nurses on humanoid robots in dementia care
sources.claim: The humanoid companion robot Abi was placed in Eskaton memory care neighborhoods for a UC Davis nursing study; in a group activity it sang a familiar song and residents joined in, with staff and researchers present.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: leading a sing-along in a care facility. Closest deployed analogue to the therapist's singing, but the output is synthesized/pre-set song audio through a speaker, with no instrument playing, key transposition or clinical adaptation, and it is framed as enhancing rather than replacing staff.

sources.title: News on Aging (ILC-Japan) – PALRO in elderly care facilities
sources.claim: PALRO, a small humanoid deployed commercially in Japanese eldercare facilities, acts as emcee for recreation sessions, leading singing, quizzes and exercise with residents.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: leading group recreation music activities inside an institution. Establishes that deployed care robots run song-based group activities, but from fixed program libraries via speaker audio, without playing instruments or adapting music to individual clinical response.

tasks.label: Assess client functioning levels, strengths, and areas of need in terms of perceptual, sensory, affective, communicative, musical, physical, cognitive, social, spiritual, or other abilities.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Initial music therapy assessment of a child with autism or a developmental disability in a school or outpatient clinic session room: therapist reviews the IEP/referral, engages the child in structured and improvisational music experiences, observes and rates communicative, motor, sensory, social, and musical responses on a tool such as IMTAP or SEMTAP, interviews the caregiver or teacher, and writes the assessment report with strengths and needs.

Assessment of an older adult with dementia in a nursing home or memory care unit: chart review, family interview about music preferences and history, observation of the resident's affect, orientation, verbal/nonverbal communication, participation and physical response to preferred and live music, followed by documentation of functioning levels and treatment recommendations.

Bedside assessment of a medical patient in acute care, inpatient rehabilitation, or hospice: brief screening at the bedside covering pain, affect, arousal/alertness, respiratory and physical status, communication ability, spiritual/existential concerns, and music preferences, completed within a short window and charted in the EHR alongside the interdisciplinary team.

Intake/assessment of adults in inpatient psychiatric or substance-use treatment, often during a group session: therapist evaluates affect, mood, insight, impulse control, social interaction, coping skills, and verbal/musical expression during and after music experiences, cross-references clinical records, and records findings on the unit's assessment form.

Assessment of a private-practice or community client (e.g., adult with intellectual disability, neurologic rehab client, or home-based client): interview with client and family, music preference and history inventory, observation of speech, gait/motor function, cognition and mood during musical tasks, and preparation of a written assessment for funders or referring clinicians.

tasks.label: Observe and document client reactions, progress, or other outcomes related to music therapy.

tasks.label: Improvise instrumentally, vocally, or physically to meet client's therapeutic needs.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Group session in a long-term care or memory-care facility: the therapist improvises guitar or keyboard accompaniment for 6-15 residents, changing key, tempo, and rhythm live to match residents' spontaneous singing, breathing, and movement, hands out and re-tunes percussion, and shifts material when a resident becomes agitated or withdrawn.

Individual session with a child with autism or a developmental disability in a school or outpatient clinic: the therapist mirrors and matches the child's spontaneous drumming, vocalizations, and body movement, improvises on piano/guitar to build turn-taking and joint attention, and physically prompts or moves with the child.

Hospital bedside (NICU, oncology, palliative/hospice unit): the therapist improvises live singing and guitar entrained to the patient's respiration rate and observed state, adjusting dynamics and harmonic tension around monitors, lines, and staff interruptions, sometimes with family present.

Behavioral-health or psychiatric session (individual or group): client-led free improvisation on drums, piano, or tuned percussion; the therapist responds musically in real time, matching or contrasting to hold structure, contain affect, and manage safety, then brings the improvisation to a close.

Home or community visit (in-home hospice, early intervention, community day program): the therapist improvises vocally and on a portable instrument in an uncontrolled room, working around furniture, pets, family members, and whatever sound-makers are at hand.
Telehealth session from a clinic room: the therapist improvises vocally and on guitar/keyboard over video, adapting to the client's audio-delayed responses and on-screen movement.

sources.developer: Georgia Tech Center for Music Technology / Robotic Musicianship Lab (Gil Weinberg)
sources.title: Music, body, and machine: gesture-based synchronization in human-robot musical interaction (Frontiers in Robotics and AI)
sources.claim: Shimon, Georgia Tech's robotic marimba player, autonomously improvises music in real time in response to human collaborators, using rule-based and learned models of improvisation.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: real-time musical improvisation responsive to a human partner's playing. It is the closest demonstrated robotic capability to a therapist's clinical improvisation, but the partner is a trained musician supplying clear harmonic/rhythmic input, the instrument is a single fixed marimba, and no assessment of a client's affect or therapeutic goals is involved.

sources.developer: Georgia Tech Center for Music Technology
sources.title: Shimon | Center for Music Technology - Georgia Tech
sources.claim: Shimon's improvisation has been shown repeatedly in live performance settings with human musicians at concerts and festivals, i.e., on stages rather than in clinical sessions.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: live improvised musical interaction with humans. Establishes the environment in which the only autonomous improvising music robot actually works — a concert stage with musicians — not a therapy room with a client.

sources.developer: University of Denver Computer Vision and Social Robotics Lab (Feng, Mahoor, Dino)
sources.title: A Music-Therapy Robotic Platform for Children With Autism: A Pilot Study (Frontiers in Robotics and AI)
sources.claim: An autonomous NAO-based music-therapy platform localizes and plays a xylophone and runs music-based turn-taking and imitation activities with autistic children in a lab/clinic room, but it plays customized pre-composed songs and scores imitation rather than improvising.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robot-delivered music therapy activity with a clinical population. Shows the state of the art for autonomous music-based clinical interaction — instrument playing of fixed composed material plus imitation scoring — and therefore what is not yet demonstrated: improvisation generated to meet the client's therapeutic needs.

sources.developer: Yale University (Scassellati lab; Matheus, Ghose et al.)
sources.title: Exploring robot-led activities between people living with dementia and family care partners (Frontiers in Robotics and AI)
sources.claim: The socially assistive robot Ommie has been adapted to lead shared breathing and singing wellness activities with people living with dementia and their ... partners; the activities are designed scripts, and the robot does not play instruments or improvise music.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robot-led musical/wellness activity with a dementia population. Directly relevant population and setting, but the musical content is pre-designed rather than improvised, so it does not substantiate improvisation to meet a client's needs.

sources.system: Oscar (keyboard) and Polaris (drums) humanoid music robots
sources.developer: University research team (published in PeerJ Computer Science)
sources.title: Integrating humanoid robots with human musicians for synchronized musical performances (PeerJ Computer Science)
sources.claim: Recent humanoid musical robots performing with human musicians still depend on a human operator to initiate and control the musical sequence, with the second robot merely following tempo cues.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic ensemble playing alongside human musicians. Shows that outside of Shimon, contemporary instrument-playing humanoids are operator-driven, which bears on whether an autonomous machine could sustain responsive improvisation with a client.

tasks.label: Plan or structure music therapy sessions to achieve appropriate transitions, pacing, sequencing, energy level, or intensity in accordance with treatment plans.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Inpatient behavioral health or psychiatric unit: therapist plans a 45-minute group session for 6-10 adults, sequencing a low-arousal opening (breath-paced listening), a mid-session active drumming or songwriting segment for affect expression, and a de-escalating closure, with intensity ceilings set by patient acuity and unit safety rules; plan is written into the session outline and tied to charted goals.

School or pediatric clinic: therapist structures a 30-minute individual session for a child with autism or developmental delay, sequencing greeting song, a turn-taking instrument activity, a high-energy movement-to-music segment, and a predictable transition/closing song, with pacing and sensory intensity calibrated to IEP objectives and the child's arousal tolerance.

Long-term care or memory care: therapist plans a group or individual session for older adults with dementia, sequencing familiar preferred music for orientation and reminiscence, gradually raising energy for a rhythmic movement segment, then tapering to calm closure to avoid agitation at transition back to the unit; plan follows the care plan's behavioral and mood goals.

Medical hospital bedside (NICU, oncology infusion, palliative/hospice): therapist plans a short, highly flexible session for one patient, choosing entrainment tempo, dynamic range, and intensity from the patient's clinical status and pain/anxiety goals, and pre-planning contingency branches for interruptions by clinical care.

Private practice or community program caseload planning: therapist blocks out weekly plans across a mixed caseload, sequencing materials and activity arcs for each client, adjusting pacing and intensity from the prior session's documentation, and preparing repertoire and instrument sets in advance of the week.

tasks.label: Engage clients in music experiences to identify client responses to different styles of music, types of musical experiences, such as improvising or listening, or elements of music, such as tempo or harmony.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: School or special-education therapy room: individual or small-group session with a child with autism or a developmental disability. Therapist carries in and distributes hand drums, shakers and a guitar, alternates live improvisation, preferred-song singing and listening, varies tempo/style/harmony, and reads vocalizations, eye contact, motor initiation and agitation to document responses for IEP or treatment goals.

Hospital bedside (medical/surgical, pediatric, oncology, NICU or acute rehab): patient in bed with IV lines and monitors, family sometimes present. Therapist brings guitar and small percussion, offers different genres and live entrained tempi versus recorded listening, hands instruments to the patient, and observes affect, breathing, pain behavior and physiological change in real time.

Long-term care / memory-care activity room: group of 8-15 residents, some in wheelchairs, with varying hearing and cognition. Therapist performs live familiar songs from different eras and styles, passes out hand percussion, shifts tempo and harmony, and tracks each resident's engagement, singing, movement or agitation to identify which musical elements elicit response.

Behavioral health setting (inpatient psychiatric unit or outpatient clinic): individual or group session using clinical improvisation on drums and keyboard, patient-selected music listening and lyric discussion. Therapist observes affect, interaction, mood shifts and safety concerns during and after each music experience and documents responses.

Home-based, hospice-in-home or community private-practice session: client's own living room or bedroom, layout differing site to site, family members and pets present, ambient noise and clutter. Therapist sets up portable instruments where space allows, offers listening versus live improvisation, and notes which styles and experiences produce relaxation, engagement or distress.

sources.system: NAO music-therapy robotic platform (University of Denver)
sources.title: A Music-Therapy Robotic Platform for Children With Autism: A Pilot Study (Frontiers in Robotics and AI)
sources.claim: An autonomous NAO-based music-therapy platform localizes and plays a xylophone with its arms and runs music imitation/turn-taking intervention sessions with children with ASD, classifying arousal from wearable EDA signals; it is a research pilot, not a clinical assessment service.
sources.transferJustification: Closest published analogue to this task: a robot engaging a client in a music experience and measuring the client's response. It does not transfer, because the scenario is a single fixed instrument and imitation game, with sensors on the child, and yields no therapist-grade identification of responses to styles, experiences or musical elements.

sources.system: NAO music-therapy robotic platform (University of Denver)
sources.title: A Music-Therapy Robotic Platform for Children With Autism: A Pilot Study (Frontiers in Robotics and AI)
sources.claim: The same NAO music-therapy pilot ran only inside a small climate-controlled laboratory with a trained researcher conducting baseline and exit sessions, i.e. a purpose-built research setting rather than a clinic, school or bedside.
sources.transferJustification: Establishes the environment and supervision conditions of the only autonomous music-therapy robot found, showing the demonstration does not cover unsupervised sessions in human care settings.

sources.title: Hospitals Deploying Robot Programmed to Act Like Child to Comfort Pediatric Patients (Futurism)
sources.claim: Robin the Robot is deployed in US pediatric hospitals and nursing homes for emotional support and plays patients' favorite songs, but the great majority of its behavior is produced by remote human teleoperators rather than autonomously.
sources.transferJustification: Nearest deployed system in the same settings (hospital, nursing home) that uses music to elicit patient response; it cannot support a positive judgment because it is predominantly teleoperated and performs no clinical identification of responses.

sources.developer: Georgia Tech Center for Music Technology (Gil Weinberg)
sources.title: Shimon | Center for Music Technology - Georgia Tech
sources.claim: Shimon is an autonomous improvising marimba robot that perceives and improvises with human musicians in real time, demonstrated in concerts and festivals with trained performers, not in clinical assessment sessions with patients.
sources.transferJustification: Related task is live musical improvisation with a human partner, one component of this task. Transfer fails: Shimon is a fixed stage instrument playing with skilled musicians, cannot hand instruments to a patient, adapt to nonverbal clinical cues, or document client responses.

sources.title: QTrobot in Behavioral Therapy for Autistic Children - LuxAI S.A.
sources.claim: QTrobot, a commercially deployed social robot used in autism therapy in clinics and schools, functions as a mediator within therapist-led sessions and a data-capture aid, not as an autonomous replacement for the clinician conducting and interpreting the session.
sources.transferJustification: Related task is robot-assisted therapy activity delivery in schools/clinics. It does not substantiate completion here: the human therapist still runs and interprets the session, and no music-assessment output is produced by the robot alone.
