tasks.label: Set up, clean, and maintain laboratory equipment.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Hospital core lab, day shift start: perform daily startup/shutdown maintenance on the high-volume chemistry/immunoassay analyzer line (probe and cuvette washes, priming, system checks, calibration readiness) so the line is released for patient testing.

Hands-on daily/weekly maintenance on the other bench analyzers (hematology, coagulation, urinalysis, blood gas, automated stainers): run cleaning-solution cycles, wipe sampler probes and needles, check and empty waste traps and containers, swap reagent/wash bottles and tubing, record in the maintenance log.

Scheduled preventive and corrective maintenance per manufacturer schedule: disassemble and clean probes, mixers and nozzles, replace tubing, syringes, filters, seals and lamps, unclog aspiration lines after a clot, reassemble, re-verify with QC and document.

Setting an instrument up for the run: stage and load reagent packs/bottles, consumables (cuvette segments, tips, cells) and calibrator/control materials into the analyzer, start startup, priming and calibration routines, and confirm the instrument is ready.

Cleaning and decontamination around the bench: wipe analyzer exteriors, benches and biosafety cabinet interiors with disinfectant, clean a centrifuge chamber and rotor after a tube breakage, clean microscope stage/optics, set up and clean ancillary equipment (water baths, incubators), and wash/autoclave reusable labware.

Satellite/point-of-care or physician-office lab: upkeep of small benchtop and cartridge analyzers - wipe-down with disinfectant, run electronic QC/simulator checks, replace cartridges and printer supplies, minor troubleshooting between patient visits.

tasks.label: Operate, calibrate, or maintain equipment used in quantitative or qualitative analysis, such as spectrophotometers, calorimeters, flame photometers, or computer-controlled analyzers.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Hospital core laboratory, day shift: operating the high-throughput chemistry/immunoassay line (analyzers connected to a track or workcell) through the routine specimen workload — presenting/loading tubes, starting and monitoring runs, routing samples, reruns and dilutions, unloading and archiving tubes.

Running scheduled calibration and quality control on automated analyzers: presenting calibrator and control vials, launching the calibration/QC run per assay schedule, evaluating results against Westgard-type rules, accepting the calibration or repeating it before patient testing resumes.

Scheduled preventive maintenance and consumable replenishment on analyzers: daily/weekly/monthly probe and cuvette cleaning, wiping and decontaminating, replacing reagent packs, syringes, tubing, filters, ISE modules and lamps, emptying waste, priming lines, and logging the maintenance record.

Operating standalone bench analyzers in specialty sections of a mid-size hospital lab (hematology, coagulation, urinalysis, blood gas, microbiology plating/ID): loading racks or specimens, running the batch, and handling the plates/slides/target plates the instrument produces.

Semi-manual bench work with photometric instruments: hand pipetting samples, standards and reagents into cuvettes or microplates, dilutions, incubation and washing, then reading absorbance on a spectrophotometer/microplate reader and calculating results.

Troubleshooting an instrument fault mid-run: clot or short-sample error at the probe, drifting QC, error codes, swapping a failed part or probe, re-priming, re-calibrating and re-running affected specimens under time pressure.

tasks.label: Select and prepare specimens and media for cell cultures, using aseptic technique and knowledge of medium components and cell requirements.

instances.label: Hospital/reference clinical microbiology bench: technologist receives routine liquid-based specimens (urine tubes, ESwabs, liquefied sputum, stool in transport vials), selects the media set required for that source and order (blood, MacConkey, chocolate, selective/chromogenic agars, enrichment broth), inoculates and streaks for isolation using aseptic technique, labels plates, and sends them to incubation. High volume, routine, standard containers.

Media/reagent preparation room of a hospital or reference lab: weighing dehydrated media powder, dissolving in purified water, sterilizing/autoclaving, tempering, adding heat-labile supplements, pouring plates or dispensing broth tubes, and running sterility/growth QC before release to the bench.

Cytogenetics / tissue-culture setup in a biosafety cabinet: selecting the appropriate complete medium (e.g., RPMI with FBS, mitogen, or amnio medium) for a peripheral blood, bone marrow, amniotic ... or product-of-conception specimen, aseptically transferring the specimen into flasks/coverslip dishes, gassing/incubating, then feeding and subculturing over days.

Mycobacteriology / virology work in a BSL-2 or BSL-3 room: NALC-NaOH digestion-decontamination of sputum and other specimens, neutralization, high-speed centrifugation, resuspension of the pellet, inoculation of supplemented liquid broth (MGIT with OADC/PANTA) and solid slants, or inoculation of viral transport fluid into shell-vial cell monolayers.

Irregular and difficult specimens on the bench: tissue biopsies, bone, hardware/implants, aspirates and large-volume body fluids. Technologist assesses gross adequacy, selects the representative portion, mince/grinds or homogenizes it aseptically, then chooses and inoculates an expanded media set including anaerobic and fungal media.

tasks.label: Obtain, cut, stain, and mount biological material on slides for microscopic study and diagnosis, following standard laboratory procedures.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Hospital hematology laboratory: technologist takes EDTA whole-blood tubes flagged by the analyzer (including high/low WBC, blast-containing, and pediatric samples), makes a wedge peripheral blood film, labels it, air-dries, Wright/Wright-Giemsa stains and rinses it, and delivers a readable film for morphology review, usually within the shift's turnaround window.

Clinical microbiology laboratory: from sputum, wound swabs, urine, sterile body fluids and positive blood-culture bottles, the technologist pipettes or rolls a measured amount of specimen into a defined area of a labeled glass slide, fixes it (heat or methanol), Gram stains it, and reads/reports the smear, often STAT for positive blood cultures.

Hospital or reference anatomic pathology histology lab: processed tissue is embedded in paraffin blocks with correct orientation, faced and sectioned at ~4 um on a microtome, ribbons floated on a warm water bath, picked up on labeled slides, dried, H&E stained and coverslipped; blocks range from large uniform sections to tiny needle biopsies and fatty/calcified tissue.

Anatomic pathology / immunohistochemistry lab: cutting additional unstained sections from existing blocks onto charged slides and running special stains (GMS, trichrome, AFB, iron) or IHC/ISH panels with controls, then coverslipping and checking control quality before release to the pathologist.

Cytology lab: non-gynecologic fluid specimens (urine, pleural/peritoneal/pericardial fluid, FNA rinses, bronchial washings, low-cellularity CSF) are aliquoted, concentrated by centrifuge or cytocentrifuge or processed as liquid-based vials, transferred as a monolayer to a labeled slide, fixed, Pap or Wright stained, and coverslipped.

General bench/STAT work: KOH and saline wet mounts, fungal preps, fecal concentrate ova-and-parasite slides, urine sediment and semen preparations, Tzanck smears - a drop of variable, sometimes viscous or particulate material is placed on a slide, coverslipped by hand, occasionally stained, and read immediately; volumes are small and specimen containers are non-standard.

instances.label: Verification/validation of a new or modified assay on an automated analyzer in a hospital core lab (chemistry, immunoassay, hematology, coagulation): pull leftover patient specimens and QC material, run precision replicates, build serial dilutions for linearity/AMR, run a 20-40 sample method comparison against the current method, evaluate against CLIA/CAP acceptance criteria, write the validation summary and SOP.

Developing or optimizing a laboratory-developed test in molecular or mass-spec sections: primer/probe titration, master-mix and extraction optimization, thermal-cycling or chromatographic condition screening, limit-of-detection dilution series, iterative parameter changes based on amplification curves or chromatograms, then locking down and documenting the final procedure.

Standardizing or modifying a manual/semi-manual bench procedure: adjusting incubation, wash and dilution steps in a manual ELISA or extraction; qualifying a new reagent lot or diluent; adapting a published method to in-house equipment; running the comparison plates/tubes, reading results, and revising the written procedure.

Investigating and modifying an existing procedure that is drifting or failing: repeated QC outliers, discrepant or clinically implausible results, interference or carryover complaints. The tech isolates the cause across reagent, calibrator, instrument, water, pipette and technique, changes the procedure or maintenance step, and verifies the fix with re-runs.

Evaluating methods in microbiology or transfusion service: comparing culture media, inoculum volumes or streaking patterns, qualifying a new organism ID/AST platform, or validating gel-card versus tube antiglobulin methods; involves plating, subculture, colony picking, incubation/reading of plates or agglutination reactions across many clinical isolates or samples.

tasks.label: Cultivate, isolate, or assist in identifying microbial organisms or perform various tests on these microorganisms.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Routine high-volume specimen setup in a hospital/reference clinical microbiology lab: barcoded liquid-based specimens (urine, ESwabs from wounds/throat/genital sites, liquefied respiratory, stool) are planted and streaked for isolation onto selective and non-selective agar plates, labeled and racked for incubation.

Incubation and first-look plate reading: loading plates into CO2/aerobic incubators, retrieving them at fixed time points, screening growth versus no-growth, counting colonies for urine cultures, screening chromogenic MRSA/GBS/strep plates, and releasing negatives.

Isolate work-up and identification: picking discrete colonies from mixed-growth plates, spotting MALDI-TOF target slides with matrix (or setting up biochemical/ID cards), and running the identification to a reportable species result.

Antimicrobial susceptibility testing: preparing a standardized 0.5 McFarland suspension from isolated colonies, inoculating Mueller-Hinton plates or AST cards, applying disks, incubating, and measuring/interpreting zones or MICs against breakpoints.

Complex or non-liquid specimens handled at the bench in a biosafety cabinet: tissue and bone grinding/homogenization, mycobacterial sputum digestion-decontamination and AFB smears, fungal cultures needing subculture and microscopic morphology, anaerobic plating and workup.

Positive blood culture workup: transferring broth from the flagged bottle, preparing and staining a Gram smear, subculturing onto plates, and driving rapid identification and susceptibility from the positive bottle for a STAT call to the clinician.

instances.label: Hospital/reference cytogenetics lab: constitutional peripheral blood lymphocyte cultures (PHA-stimulated, 72 h in 15 mL tubes in a CO2 incubator). Tech blocks with Colcemid for a set interval, then harvests — centrifuge, aspirate supernatant, add pre-warmed hypotonic KCl, timed swelling, add Carnoy's fixative dropwise with resuspension, 2-3 fix washes — producing a clean fixed cell suspension with high mitotic index ready for slide dropping. Batches of 20-60 tubes per day.

Oncology cytogenetics: unstimulated bone marrow aspirates and neoplastic peripheral bloods set up as direct/24 h/48 h cultures. Harvest time is chosen from specimen type, cellularity and diagnosis (fast-cycling leukemic cells need shorter Colcemid exposure); low-cellularity or clotted/particulate specimens need adjusted hypotonic and fixation, and reduced aspiration to avoid pellet loss.

Prenatal in-situ cultures: amniotic fluid or CVS grown on coverslips in small Petri dishes (or chamber slides). Tech inspects colonies daily on an inverted phase microscope, judges when colonies have enough mitoses, adds Colcemid, then harvests in situ on the dish — hypotonic, fixative changes, controlled drying — without disturbing colony architecture.

Adherent flask cultures — products of conception, skin fibroblasts, solid tumor: tech monitors growth/confluence and mitotic activity by inverted microscope, decides when the culture is at optimum log-phase growth, adds Colcemid, detaches cells with trypsin/EDTA from the flask, then completes a suspension harvest (hypotonic, fixation, washes).

Other cultured-cell harvests supporting hospital/reference lab testing (e.g., cell lines or primary cultures maintained in T-flasks or plates for cell-based assays, tissue-culture-based virology, or cell-processing support): technologist tracks confluence/growth phase and harvests the monolayer at the optimum point for the downstream test.

instances.label: Constitutional peripheral blood for routine karyotype: in a hospital/reference cytogenetics lab, aseptically inoculate whole blood into mitogen-containing media in tubes/flasks, incubate ~72 h, add colcemid, harvest (hypotonic KCl, methanol:acetic fixation, washes), drop and age slides, then trypsin/Giemsa G-band and coverslip so analyzable metaphases are ready for the analyst.

Oncology bone marrow aspirate or leukemic peripheral blood: assess cellularity/count, set up direct and 24/48 h unstimulated cultures in media, harvest by hypotonic/fixation, wash pellets, drop slides, G-band, and reserve fixed pellet for FISH — often on a same-day/STAT timeline with small or bloody samples.

Prenatal amniotic fluid: centrifuge the fluid, resuspend and seed in-situ coverslip dishes and/or backup flasks, feed and monitor colony growth microscopically, then harvest in situ (colcemid, hypotonic, fixative on the coverslips) and stain for banding, under sterile technique and strict specimen-identity control.

Slide-based FISH preparation: from fixed cell suspensions (blood/marrow) or FFPE tumor sections, prepare slides (dropping/sectioning), pretreat/deparaffinize, apply probe, denature and hybridize overnight, perform stringency washes, counterstain with DAPI and coverslip, producing hybridized slides ready for signal enumeration.

Solid tumor biopsy or products of conception tissue: in a biosafety cabinet, inspect the specimen, dissect away necrotic/non-representative material, mince viable tissue with scalpels, digest with collagenase, then set up flask or coverslip cultures, feed them, and harvest for chromosome preparation.

Chorionic villus sample: under a stereomicroscope, pick and clean villi free of maternal decidua and blood clot in a dish, split material for direct/short-term preparation and long-term culture, then harvest and prepare slides for banding.

tasks.label: Examine chromosomes found in biological specimens to detect abnormalities.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Constitutional/postnatal case: G-banded metaphase slides from a peripheral blood culture (suspected aneuploidy, infertility, recurrent loss). Technologist scans slides at the microscope/imaging station, counts chromosomes in ~20 metaphases, fully karyotypes 5, and judges numerical and structural abnormalities (translocations, deletions, inversions, markers) at ~550-band level for an ISCN result.

Prenatal case: amniotic fluid or CVS cultures, G-banded slides. Colony-by-colony analysis for mosaicism, counting/karyotyping the required cells, distinguishing true mosaicism from culture artifact, under tight turnaround for a clinical decision.

Oncology conventional karyotype: bone marrow (AML/MDS/CML/ALL, myeloma) or solid-tumor culture. Fuzzy, short, overlapping metaphases of poor quality; analyst reconstructs complex/composite karyotypes, clonal subclones and cryptic rearrangements from a handful of analyzable cells.

Oncology interphase FISH panel: hybridized slides (e.g., CLL 4-probe panel, myeloma CD138-selected, BCR::ABL1 dual-fusion MRD). Scoring 200-500 nuclei per probe on a fluorescence microscope or scanner, classifying signal patterns, applying cutoffs, reporting percent abnormal nuclei.

Targeted FISH slides in a clinical lab: rapid prenatal aneuploidy FISH on uncultured amniocytes (X, Y, 13, 18, 21), UroVysion urine FISH, or HER2/tissue FISH. Enumerate signals in a defined number of nuclei and call normal vs abnormal against kit criteria.

Array case (aCGH/SNP microarray): scanned array data reviewed for copy-number and LOH aberrations; assess QC metrics, separate true imbalances from noise and benign CNVs, define breakpoints and mosaic levels for the case result.

tasks.label: Prepare slides of cell cultures following standard procedures.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Routine constitutional peripheral-blood lymphocyte cultures in a clinical cytogenetics lab: after colcemid arrest, the tech harvests culture tubes (hypotonic KCl, Carnoy fixative washes, centrifugation, resuspension), then drops the fixed cell suspension onto barcoded glass slides in a temperature/humidity-controlled chamber, dries them, checks spreading under phase contrast and labels the slides.

Oncology bone marrow or neoplastic peripheral blood suspension cultures (direct, 24 h, 48 h) with adequate cellularity: harvest each culture tube, resuspend the pellet to appropriate density, and drop several slides per case (some reserved for FISH), adjusting drop volume and humidity to the sample.

Prenatal amniotic fluid or CVS cultures grown in situ on glass coverslips in small Petri dishes: colcemid, hypotonic, fixative additions and aspirations performed on the dish, air-drying to yield coverslip specimens ready for banding, with strict specimen identity control.

Solid tumor, products of conception, or skin fibroblast cultures: adherent cells either harvested in situ on coverslips or detached from flasks with trypsin, then harvested and dropped as a suspension; yields and mitotic index are variable and slide density must be judged case by case.

Slide preparation for FISH from fixed cultured cell pellets: dispensing cell suspension onto marked or multi-well slides, aging/baking slides, and marking hybridization areas so the slides meet the FISH assay's density and background requirements.

Problem specimens: very small or bloody pellets, hypocellular marrow, bone biopsy fragments with particulate matter, poorly growing cultures. The tech judges cellularity by eye, concentrates or re-suspends, drops test slides, inspects under phase contrast, and re-drops or salvages the specimen to get analyzable slides.

instances.label: High-volume clinical cytogenetics lab, routine constitutional chromosomal microarray (CMA) batch: prepared patient DNA (blood/amniocyte-derived) plus reference/control is applied to the array plate or BeadChip grid, the hybridization/wash/stain/scan instrumentation is run overnight, and CEL/IDAT files with QC metrics are produced for analysis. Batch of 8-96 samples, standard validated protocol.

Small rush batch (1-8 samples), e.g., prenatal/products-of-conception CMA with a tight turnaround: a single array or a few arrays plus one control are loaded, instrumentation run on a short cycle, and analyzable data produced same/next day in a hospital cytogenetics lab.

Two-color oligo array CGH on glass slides (e.g., GenetiSure/custom aCGH): labeled patient DNA and sex-matched reference control are pipetted onto the gasket/array grid, hybridization chamber assembled and rotated overnight, slides washed, then scanned on a microarray scanner with feature extraction to produce analyzable log-ratio data.

Oncology/tumor array run in a molecular-cytogenetics lab: degraded or low-input DNA from FFPE tumor or bone marrow applied to the array (e.g., OncoScan/CytoScan), fluidics stain/wash and scanning run, CEL files and copy-number QC produced; input quality is marginal and reruns are common.

Failed or marginal run requiring troubleshooting: array shows high derivative log-ratio spread, low SNP call rate, bubbles, wash streaks or scanner artifacts; the technologist diagnoses the cause, adjusts scan settings or re-hybridizes retained target onto a fresh grid with control, and delivers an analyzable result within the reporting window.

tasks.label: Evaluate appropriateness of received specimens for requested tests.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Peripheral blood for constitutional or oncology chromosome analysis, FISH or microarray, received as a barcoded primary vacutainer (sodium heparin or EDTA) with an electronic order: technologist matches two patient identifiers on the tube to the requisition, confirms the anticoagulant/tube type is correct for the ordered test, confirms volume is adequate, confirms collection is within the stability window, and inspects the tube for leakage, hemolysis or clotting before accessioning or rejecting.

Bone marrow aspirate for leukemia/MDS karyotype and FISH panels, hand-delivered from an OR or hematology clinic in a green-top sodium heparin tube or a capped syringe, often with a paper requisition: technologist judges whether the 1-3 mL is adequate and unclotted, whether the marrow is heavily blood-diluted or a near-dry tap, whether it is within 24 hours of collection and correctly anticoagulated, and whether enough material exists for the full panel plus concurrent flow/molecular orders.

Prenatal specimens: 20+ mL amniotic fluid in sterile syringes or conical tubes, or a chorionic villus sample in transport medium: technologist checks volume against the ordered combination of karyotype/array/FISH, inspects for blood-tinged or brown discoloration and container/sterility problems, confirms gestational age, indication and twin labeling, and for CVS inspects the sample under a dissecting scope for sufficient villi and separates maternal decidua before accepting.

Fresh tissue specimens - products of conception, fetal tissue, skin biopsy, solid tumor or lymph node - arriving in transport medium or saline in varied containers: technologist assesses whether enough viable tissue is present for culture or array, whether it was wrongly placed in formalin or frozen (reject), whether it is grossly contaminated or dried out, and whether the requested test suits the tissue submitted.

FFPE material for FISH (HER2, ALK, MYC, etc.): paraffin block plus unstained slides and a marked H&E arriving from an outside pathology department: technologist verifies block/slide labels match the case and requisition, counts and checks slide/section quality, checks fixative type and block age, and confirms the marked tumor area contains enough tumor cells for the ordered probe, else requests recuts or rejects.

tasks.label: Count numbers of chromosomes and identify the structural abnormalities by viewing culture slides through microscopes, light microscopes, or photomicroscopes.

instances.label: Routine constitutional peripheral-blood G-banded case in a clinical cytogenetics lab: load/scan culture slides on a brightfield microscope, screen and select analyzable metaphases, count chromosomes in ~20 cells, analyze ~5 band-by-band and karyotype 2-3, ruling in/out translocations, inversions, deletions, markers; result written in ISCN for director sign-out.

Prenatal amniotic fluid or CVS culture slides: colony-by-colony metaphase counting and analysis at high band resolution under a light microscope, assessment of possible mosaicism and pseudomosaicism, subtle structural rearrangement detection, under a tight turnaround-time requirement.

Bone marrow / leukemia-lymphoma culture slides: 20-cell count and analysis of short, fuzzy, poorly spread chromosomes with low band resolution; identification of complex clonal structural abnormalities (translocations, deletions, marker and ring chromosomes) and definition of clones/subclones.

Products of conception, solid tumor, or other tissue cultures: few, poor-quality metaphases, debris and overlap, possible maternal cell contamination; technologist must scan the slide extensively under the scope to find and analyze any countable cells.

FISH slide review on cultured cells under a fluorescence microscope: enumerate signals in 100-200 interphase nuclei and/or examine metaphase FISH to confirm or characterize a numerical/structural abnormality (e.g., BCR::ABL1 fusion, del(17p), trisomy 12) against lab cutoffs.

instances.label: Routine peripheral blood or bone marrow aspirate for constitutional or oncology chromosomal microarray: technologist batches barcoded EDTA tubes, runs a benchtop automated nucleic acid extractor (QIAsymphony/chemagic/MagNA Pure) or spin columns, quantifies gDNA (fluorometer/spectrophotometer), dilutes each sample to the target ng/uL, labels aliquot tubes, and stages them for array set-up. High volume, standard clinical lab bench.

Array target preparation proper: normalized gDNA pipetted into a 24/96-well plate and taken through the array kit protocol (restriction digest, ligation, PCR/whole-genome amplification, bead purification, fragmentation, fluorescent or biotin labeling, hybridization cocktail) and loaded onto the microarray slide/plate, with thermal cyclers, shakers and magnets, per CytoScan/OncoScan, Infinium or Agilent aCGH SOPs.

Cultured or fresh cellular specimens: harvested amniocyte/CVS/POC or bone-marrow culture cell pellets and fresh solid tumor tissue; pellet resuspension or tissue disruption, proteinase K lysis, extraction, quantification, dilution and labeling. Smaller irregular batches, variable input amounts, prenatal STAT turnaround.

FFPE tumor blocks/sections for oncology arrays with adequate tumor content: deparaffinization, extended proteinase K digestion, magnetic-bead or column extraction, quantification and dilution to the kit's input requirement, tube labeling and hand-off to array prep.

Problem specimens: marginal or degraded yield, clotted or scant sample, inhibitor carry-over or failed QC ratios; the technologist judges whether to re-extract residual specimen, concentrate by vacuum/bead clean-up, switch chemistry, apply whole-genome amplification, or reject the sample and request a redraw, then reworks it to an acceptable array input.

Identification and logistics tied to the prep: printing and applying accession barcode labels to extraction tubes, aliquots and array plates, verifying tube ID against the LIS worklist, recording concentrations/QC values, and racking residual DNA into the freezer/biobank for repeats.

instances.label: Peripheral blood culture setup in a clinical cytogenetics lab: verify barcoded sodium-heparin tubes against the requisition, judge specimen quality/volume, select the culture protocol (e.g., PHA-stimulated 72 h for constitutional studies, unstimulated or B-cell-stimulated for hematologic panels), and aseptically dispense set volumes of blood into pre-warmed media tubes/flasks in a biosafety cabinet, then cap, label, log and incubate. Highest-volume, most routine instance.

Bone marrow / leukemia specimen culture setup: assess a small, often clotted or hypocellular aspirate, perform a nucleated cell count, dilute to target density, and set up several parallel cultures (direct/overnight, 24 h, 48 h, synchronized, mitogen-stimulated) each with different media and additives, aseptically in a biosafety cabinet, under STAT turnaround pressure.

Amniotic fluid culture setup: aseptically transfer fluid from transport syringes/tubes (discarding the first aliquot), centrifuge, resuspend the small cell pellet in amniocyte medium, seed both in-situ coverslip dishes and back-up flasks, gas and incubate; sterility is critical because the specimen is irreplaceable.

Solid tumor, products-of-conception, or chorionic villus tissue: inspect the tissue grossly (and under a dissecting scope for CVS), select viable, non-necrotic, non-maternal tissue, trim and mince with scalpel/scissors, enzymatically disaggregate, and plate the disaggregate into flasks/coverslip dishes with appropriate medium, aseptically.

Media and reagent preparation and QC: combine base medium with serum, L-glutamine, antibiotics and mitogens per formulation, sterile-filter, aliquot into culture tubes/bottles, label with lot and expiry, record preparation, and run sterility/growth-support QC checks; also select and warm the correct pre-made commercial media for the day's specimens.

instances.label: Routine G-banding (GTG) of metaphase slides from peripheral-blood and amniotic-fluid cultures in a hospital/reference cytogenetics lab: a batch of ~10-40 aged slides is given a timed trypsin dip, rinsed, stained in buffered Giemsa, rinsed, air-dried, and checked under the microscope for band resolution.

G-banding of bone-marrow and solid-tumor slides whose slide/chromosome quality varies batch to batch: trypsin and Giemsa times must be tuned per harvest, a pilot slide is checked, and over/under-banded slides are sometimes destained and restained.
Small-batch or STAT staining at the bench in a low-volume or research lab: one to a few slides hand-dipped in Coplin jars with a timer, blotted and dried, turnaround measured in minutes.

FISH slides (metaphase/interphase preparations after hybridization): post-hybridization stringency washes, then application of DAPI/antifade counterstain to make chromosomes and nuclei visible, coverslipping and sealing before fluorescence microscopy.

Specialty chromosome stains: C-banding (acid/barium hydroxide/hot 2xSSC then Giemsa), silver NOR staining, DAPI/distamycin, and plain solid Giemsa or Wright stain for chromosome counts and dicentric scoring.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Routine constitutional study: G-banded peripheral-blood slides in a hospital/reference cytogenetics lab. Slides are loaded onto the imaging system, scanned at low power for metaphases, ~20 high-resolution (63x/100x oil) metaphase images captured per case, and karyograms generated for the case file.

Oncology study: G-banded bone-marrow (leukemia/MDS) slides. Metaphases are sparse, fuzzy and often overlapped; multiple slides per case are scanned, 20+ usable metaphase images captured and karyograms produced despite variable spread quality.

Prenatal study: amniotic fluid or CVS cultured in situ on coverslips (or flask/slide preparations). Colony-based scanning and image capture from a required number of independent colonies, under urgent turnaround.

FISH imaging: capture of multi-fluorochrome interphase and metaphase FISH images (DAPI plus 2-3 probe channels) on blood, marrow or tissue slides at 63x/100x oil, documenting representative signal patterns for the report.

Difficult/ad-hoc capture: solid tumor, POC, or badly degraded preparations with only two or three analyzable cells, plus relocation and manual capture of a specific abnormal cell noticed by the technologist during direct microscope analysis, with image enhancement to document the aberration.

instances.label: End-of-case slide archiving in a hospital/reference cytogenetics lab: the technologist gathers the G-banded metaphase slides and FISH slides for a completed case, checks each label/accession against the case, and files them into slide folders, trays or cabinets (FISH slides into a dark -20 C box), recording the storage location so slides can be pulled during the CAP/CLIA retention period.

Archiving residual study material: capping and labeling tubes of fixed cell suspension (and, for FISH/aCGH cases, residual DNA or cell pellets), placing them in numbered positions in freezer boxes/racks in the lab's -20 C or -80 C freezer, and logging box/position in the freezer inventory for the required retention interval.

Electronic archiving at the lab workstation: saving/exporting the final karyograms, FISH/aCGH images, analysis worksheets and the signed report into the imaging/case database and LIS record with correct case identifiers and retention metadata, and confirming the backup/long-term image archive captured them.

Paper case file work: assembling the requisition, culture and harvest worksheets, printed karyograms and signed report into a case folder, filing it in the department's file cabinet, and periodically boxing, labeling and indexing older folders for long-term or off-site records storage.

Scheduled retention review and purge: pulling slides, fixed-cell tubes and case folders whose retention period has expired from the archive, documenting the disposition, and discarding them as biohazard/confidential waste while keeping the inventory records consistent.

tasks.label: Select appropriate methods of preparation and storage of media to maintain potential of hydrogen (pH), sterility, or ability to support growth.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Clinical cytogenetics lab, prenatal section: preparing complete culture medium for amniotic fluid/CVS cultures - aseptically supplementing base medium (e.g., AmnioMAX/Chang) with serum, L-glutamine and antibiotics inside a biosafety cabinet, mixing, aliquoting into sterile bottles/flasks, labeling with lot and expiry, and refrigerating at 2-8 C with caps tight to hold bicarbonate-buffered pH.

Constitutional/oncology section: preparing and dispensing blood and bone marrow culture medium (RPMI 1640 + FBS + antibiotics, with PHA or other mitogens added as required) into pre-labeled culture tubes/flasks for the day's specimen setups; surplus stored refrigerated and warmed to 37 C before use.

Media quality control: on each new lot or in-house batch, checking pH (phenol red color or pH meter), inspecting for turbidity/particulates, running a sterility incubation check on an aliquot, and running a growth-support/parallel-culture check (colony growth, mitotic index) before releasing or rejecting the lot; documenting results.

Receiving, inspecting and storing commercially prepared media, sera, mitogens and reagents: verifying cold-chain condition and expiry on delivery, logging lot numbers, rotating stock, placing items at 2-8 C or -20 C, monitoring and documenting refrigerator/freezer temperatures, and discarding expired or contaminated stock.

Preparing ancillary solutions whose pH/sterility govern culture and harvest quality - hypotonic KCl, fresh Carnoy's fixative, colcemid aliquots, 2xSSC and other FISH buffers - including pH adjustment with acid/base, filter sterilization, aliquoting, expiry dating and storage at the specified temperature.

sources.transferJustification: Aseptic transfer, dispensing and incubation of sterile culture medium inside robotic modules is the same manipulation class and sterility requirement as preparing and aliquoting cytogenetic culture medium.

tasks.label: Maintain laboratory equipment such as photomicroscopes, inverted microscopes, and standard darkroom equipment.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Routine cleaning of bench and inverted microscope optics in the cytogenetics reading room: removing immersion oil from 100x objectives with lens tissue and approved solvent, blowing dust from eyepieces and condenser, wiping stage and ocular surfaces, checking for fungus/scratches, and re-covering scopes at shift end.

Replacing consumables and components on fluorescence/photomicroscopy stations: swapping burned-out mercury or metal-halide arc lamps (or LED engines) in the lamphouse, logging lamp hours, changing FISH filter cubes, fuses, immersion oil bottles, camera/monitor cables, and disposing of mercury lamps per protocol.

Alignment, calibration and performance verification: setting Köhler illumination on brightfield/phase scopes, verifying fluorescence excitation intensity and filter performance with reference slides, calibrating the karyotyping/imaging workstation (magnification, shading, color), and recording results in equipment QC logs for CAP/CLIA inspection.

Upkeep of ancillary cytogenetics equipment kept in the same lab: CO2 incubator water pan changes and shelf decontamination, cleaning and rotor checks on centrifuges/cytocentrifuges, water bath and hybridization oven cleaning and temperature verification with NIST-traceable thermometers, biosafety cabinet surface decontamination and airflow checks, with logbook documentation.

Fault triage and service work: diagnosing an imaging station or scope problem (flickering lamp, focus drift, stage jam, camera fault), making minor repairs or adjustments, escalating to and escorting vendor field-service engineers, and maintaining/decommissioning legacy darkroom equipment (film processor cleaning, chemistry changes, safelight and light-tightness checks).

Pap slides examined with computer-assisted or digital assistance: an imaging system pre-selects fields of interest and the cytotechnologist reviews the 22 fields on an automated microscope, or reviews the whole-slide digital image with AI-flagged objects on a monitor, deciding whether flagged objects are truly abnormal and whether full manual review is needed.

Non-gynecologic cytology: urine, pleural/peritoneal/pericardial effusions, CSF, bronchial washings and brushings — often sparse, degenerated, or inflammatory backgrounds where the examiner must distinguish reactive mesothelial or urothelial cells from malignant cells on the basis of size, shape, nuclear detail and staining characteristics.

Fine-needle aspiration material (thyroid, lymph node, salivary gland, pancreas EUS), including rapid on-site adequacy evaluation at the procedure suite: examining direct smears for cellularity, architectural patterns (follicles, papillae, sheets) and cytologic atypia, and reporting adequacy/preliminary impression to the proceduralist within minutes.

Examination of ancillary preparations to resolve a difficult case: cell block sections, special stains and immunocytochemistry, correlating morphology across current and prior slides and with clinical/HPV history to arrive at a final morphologic interpretation.

instances.label: High-volume gyn (Pap) accessioning in a hospital or reference cytology lab: batches of barcoded ThinPrep/SurePath vials arrive with electronic orders; the tech confirms the vial label's two patient identifiers against the requisition/LIS order, accessions the case, and ensures the printed/etched slide label carries the same accession as the vial before processing.

Pre-screening verification at the screening workstation: the cytotechnologist pulls the case (slide tray or digital case list), confirms the slide accession and patient identifiers match the requisition, the LIS record and any prior cytology/HPV history, then documents the case (specimen adequacy, screening record, initials/time) in the LIS.

Non-gyn specimen log-in: urines, body fluids, sputa, brushings/washings and FNA needle rinses arriving in assorted containers (cups, syringes, tubes, sometimes handwritten labels and paper requisitions); verify two identifiers and specimen source/site, note volume and appearance, log into the LIS, and label derived tubes and slides to match.

Rapid on-site evaluation of an FNA in a procedure/endoscopy suite: verify patient identity with the proceduralist and the chart, label smears with patient ID, site and pass number as slides are handed over, and document passes, site and adequacy on the ROSE worksheet.

Discrepancy handling: an unlabeled, mislabeled, leaking or unmatched specimen, or a requisition missing data; contact the submitting clinic/EHR to confirm identity, apply the lab's relabel-or-reject policy, and document the corrective action and communication.

Non-gyn cytology case (FNA, body fluid, urine, bronchial washing): several stained smears plus cell-block H&E and special stains are assembled into a case folder with the worksheet and any prior slides pulled from the department slide archive, logged out, and carried to the pathologist's office/sign-out microscope inside the pathology department.

Digital-cytology workflow lab: slides are racked and scanned on a whole-slide cytology imager; the cytotechnologist marks the case for pathologist review so the images route to the pathologist's review station, and the glass slide is filed in the department archive so it can be pulled if the pathologist requests the glass.

STAT / rapid on-site evaluation case: freshly prepared and stained slides from a bedside FNA or bronchoscopy must reach the pathologist within minutes; the cytotechnologist hand-carries the slides to the pathologist in the procedure suite or sign-out room with a verbal handoff and immediate LIS entry.

Pathologist located off-site (reference lab or hospital-based group): the flagged slides are pulled, matched to the case, placed in a slide mailer/transport folder with the paperwork, logged into the tracking/chain-of-custody system, and staged at the lab's courier pickup station.

Non-gyn body fluids (urine, pleural/peritoneal/pericardial fluid, CSF, bronchial washings and brushings) arriving in assorted containers with variable volume, viscosity, blood and mucus: gross assessment, choice and execution of prep (cytospin, membrane filter, liquid-based, cell block), staining, then screening and preliminary interpretation with clinical correlation.

FNA material received in the laboratory (needle rinses, previously made direct smears, cell block for ancillary/immuno testing): prep and staining of rinse-derived slides and cell block, quality assessment, then screening and preliminary interpretation of thyroid, lymph node, pancreas, lung and salivary aspirates for the pathologist.

Rapid on-site evaluation in a procedure suite, endoscopy room, or radiology suite: the cytotechnologist takes the aspirate needle/syringe from the proceduralist, expresses and smears material on slides, air-dries/fixes and rapid-stains (Diff-Quik), evaluates adequacy at a benchtop microscope within a minute or two, calls the result to the physician, and triages remaining material into fixative, cell block, or flow cytometry media.

tasks.label: Examine specimens, using microscopes, to evaluate specimen quality.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: High-volume clinical cytology lab: cytotechnologist puts a liquid-based gynecologic (ThinPrep/SurePath) Pap slide on the microscope (or an imaging-system review station), scans the cell spot, and judges specimen quality per Bethesda — squamous cellularity against the ~5,000-cell minimum, obscuring blood/inflammation, and presence of transformation-zone component — recording satisfactory/unsatisfactory before or during screening.

Same lab, non-gynecologic liquid-based/cytospin preparations (urine, effusions, CSF, bronchial washings, FNA rinses): examine the slide microscopically to judge whether cellularity, preservation and background (blood, degeneration, obscuring debris) make the specimen diagnostic, and decide whether additional preparations or a cell block are needed.

Direct smears and referral/outside slides (FNA smears, anal Pap, conventional Pap smears, slides made in clinics): examine under the microscope for air-drying artifact, thick or crushed areas, poor fixation, weak or off Papanicolaou/Diff-Quik staining, broken coverslips or mislabeling, and decide to accept, re-stain/re-prepare, or report as unsatisfactory with a recollection request.

Rapid on-site evaluation in a hospital procedure suite (EBUS/endoscopy, radiology, thyroid clinic): the cytotechnologist examines freshly stained smears at a bench microscope within a minute or two of each pass and tells the proceduralist whether adequate lesional material was obtained or another pass is needed.

Routine lab quality control: examine the day's stain-QC and control slides plus a sample of routine preparations under the microscope to verify nuclear detail, cytoplasmic transparency, coverslipping and mounting, and check for cross-contamination or floaters; document findings and trigger corrective action on the stainer or processor.

tasks.label: Maintain effective laboratory operations by adhering to standards of specimen collection, preparation, or laboratory safety.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Hospital/reference cytology lab: gynecologic (Pap) specimens arrive in transport bags with requisitions; the cytotech verifies vial labels against requisition/LIS, checks specimen acceptability (volume, expiration, leakage), accessions, and runs vials on a liquid-based processor to produce labeled, fixed monolayer slides, retaining vial residual for HPV aliquot — all per written SOP and chain-of-custody standards.

Non-gynecologic specimen preparation at the bench/biosafety cabinet: urines, pleural/peritoneal fluids, CSF, bronchial washings/brushings, FNA needle rinses. Tech selects the SOP-specified method (direct smear, cytospin, liquid-based, cell block), pours/centrifuges/concentrates, prepares and fixes slides, and handles fresh potentially infectious material under BSL-2 practice.

Staining and coverslipping the day's slide batches to the Papanicolaou protocol on an automated stainer/coverslipper (or manual rack staining), verifying stain quality and slide labeling/identity before slides are released to screening.

Laboratory safety upkeep: donning/changing PPE, decontaminating benches and biosafety cabinet surfaces, segregating and removing biohazard and sharps waste, handling and replenishing xylene/alcohol/formalin, responding to spills and broken slides/vials, and completing safety checks and logs.

Instrument and reagent QC/maintenance: changing stain reagents and filters, cleaning and preventive maintenance on processors, stainers and centrifuges, running QC slides and controls, recording temperatures and QC results, and taking corrective action when an instrument or reagent drifts out of specification.

Support of specimen collection standards outside the prep bench: rapid on-site evaluation at FNA/EBUS procedures (making and staining direct smears at the procedure suite, assessing adequacy, advising the proceduralist), and educating/monitoring collection sites, rejecting improperly collected or labeled specimens and documenting corrective action.

ROSE in an interventional radiology suite for CT- or ultrasound-guided FNA of deep lesions (lung, liver, pancreas, retroperitoneal nodes): cytotech gowns/leads up, receives needles at the sterile field boundary, expels aspirate, prepares air-dried and alcohol-fixed smears, stains, rinses needles into fixative for cell block, assesses adequacy between passes.

Outpatient FNA clinic (thyroid, lymph node, salivary, breast), palpation- or bedside-ultrasound-guided: cytotech sets up the tray, labels slides, positions and reassures the patient, hands the pathologist needles/syringes and gauze, takes the loaded needle back, smears and fixes, applies post-procedure pressure and bandage, packages specimens and paperwork.

Cytotechnologist performs the palpation-guided FNA passes themselves under pathologist supervision in an FNA clinic: palpates the mass, preps skin, performs several needle passes on a live patient, then prepares and stains the smears.

Operating room / frozen-section room intraoperative work: cytotech at or beside the sterile field makes touch imprints of fresh resected tissue and sentinel lymph nodes, occasionally aspirates the specimen, stains and screens, and reports to the surgeon within minutes.

Inpatient ward or emergency department bedside FNA assist: cytotech carries a portable kit to a crowded room, works around lines and bed rails, assists the physician with an unsedated or uncooperative patient, prepares and fixes smears on the spot.

tasks.label: Adjust, maintain, or repair laboratory equipment, such as microscopes.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Daily microscope care at the screening bench in a hospital/reference cytology lab: wiping immersion oil and dust from objectives and oculars with lens tissue and solvent, setting Köhler illumination, condenser aperture, diopter and interpupillary adjustments, checking that stage and fine-focus move smoothly, occasionally swapping an illuminator or tightening a loose stage clip before a screening session.

Daily/weekly upkeep of the automated slide stainer and coverslipper: changing xylene, alcohol and stain baths, disposing of solvent waste, scraping/wiping dried stain and mounting-medium residue from nozzles, dispense heads and racks, clearing jammed slides and broken glass, replacing filters, tubing and gaskets, then running a test rack and signing the maintenance log.

Instrument-internal routine maintenance cycles on the automated cytology preparation instrument/analyzer: priming and flushing fluid paths, probe and nozzle wash cycles, deproteinization/rinse routines, automatic calibration verification, with the result recorded — the portion of maintenance that runs inside the instrument once it is started.

Maintenance and QC of the liquid-based cytology processor and imaging/scanning system (e.g., ThinPrep 5000 processor, imaging system or whole-slide scanner): emptying and reseating the waste bottle, loading/replacing filter and slide consumables and PreservCyt bottles, blowing dust and picking glass splinters off the stage and objective area with a blower, brush and tweezers, then running a calibration slide and reviewing the QC output.

Troubleshooting and minor repair when equipment malfunctions mid-run: diagnosing a flickering lamp, dim or uneven field, sticking stage, un-priming pump, leaking fitting or jammed carousel; opening covers, tightening/aligning/replacing a small part with hand tools, re-testing the instrument, and documenting the fix or escalating to the vendor service engineer.

Cleaning and upkeep of ancillary lab equipment: decontaminating the cytocentrifuge bowl, chucks and rotor, wiping down the biosafety cabinet and bench, cleaning vortexers and water baths, checking and recording refrigerator/incubator thermometer calibration, replacing worn gaskets or O-rings.

It transfers to the cytology instrument's internal maintenance cycles because it is the same class of instrument (fluidic clinical-lab analyzer), the same physical actions (probe/nozzle washing, fluid-path flushing, priming, auto-calibration), and the same environment (an institution-controlled clinical laboratory). It does not transfer to the hands-on portions (bath changes, wiping residue, glass removal, part replacement), which the same source shows still require operator intervention.

tasks.label: Examine specimens to detect abnormal hormone conditions.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Routine gynecologic cytology screening in a hospital or reference cytology lab: while screening a cervicovaginal Pap (liquid-based or conventional) slide, the cytotechnologist assesses the hormonal/maturation pattern — estrogenic effect, atrophy, cytolysis/progestational effect — and notes whether it is consistent with the patient's stated age and history.

A clinician-ordered cytohormonal evaluation: the cytotechnologist performs a maturation index, counting the proportion of parabasal, intermediate, and superficial squamous cells on a vaginal/lateral-wall smear to assess estrogen status (postmenopausal atrophy, HRT or topical estrogen response, amenorrhea or endocrine workup).

Examination performed on a computer workstation rather than a light microscope: reviewing whole-slide digital images or imaging-system-selected fields (e.g., ThinPrep/BD FocalPoint-guided review) and judging hormonal pattern and adequacy from the displayed cells.

Non-cervicovaginal specimens in which hormone-related cellular changes are assessed — urethral or urinary smears, endometrial or breast/nipple-discharge cytology, buccal smears — examined for evidence of hormonal effect or imbalance.

Discrepant or difficult cases: hormonal pattern conflicts with the clinical history (e.g., mature pattern in a postmenopausal patient, atrophic pattern obscured by inflammation or air-drying artifact); the cytotechnologist correlates with the requisition, documents the interpretation, and refers the slide to the pathologist.

roles.title: Histotechnologists
aliases: Mohs Technician (Micrographically Oriented Histographic Surgery Technician)
roles.description: Apply knowledge of health and disease causes to evaluate new laboratory techniques and procedures to examine tissue samples. Process and prepare histological slides from tissue sections for microscopic examination and diagnosis by pathologists. May solve technical or instrument problems or assist with research studies.

tasks.label: Embed tissue specimens into paraffin wax blocks, or infiltrate tissue specimens with wax.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: High-volume routine embedding of small biopsies (GI/endoscopic pinches, prostate and breast needle cores, skin punches) at the embedding center of a hospital or reference histology lab: open the processed cassette, transfer fragments with warm forceps into a metal mold, align multiple fragments on one geometric plane, fill with molten paraffin, seat the cassette ring, chill on a cold plate, pop out and scrape the block. Dozens to hundreds of blocks per shift, on a same-day/next-day turnaround.

Embedding standard-size sections taken from surgical resections (colon, uterus, breast, gallbladder, lung wedges, lymph nodes) in a hospital histology lab: tissue laid flat, largest cut surface down, in standard base molds; some pieces fatty, friable, or curled and needing to be flattened before the wax sets.

Infiltrating specimens with wax on the automated tissue processor: assembling cassettes into baskets/magazines, loading the retort, selecting and starting the dehydration-clearing-paraffin-infiltration protocol (overnight or rapid), monitoring the run, rotating/topping reagents and paraffin, unloading hot cassettes, and checking that tissue is adequately infiltrated before embedding.

Orientation-critical embedding in a histology lab: skin ellipses and shave/punch biopsies embedded on edge, tubular structures (fallopian tube, appendix, artery, vas) placed cross-sectionally, GI mucosa stood on its edge, oriented resection margins inked and embedded to a specified face. Errors force re-embedding or produce non-diagnostic sections.

Special and difficult blocks in a hospital or academic lab: mega/whole-mount cassettes (prostatectomy, breast lumpectomy), decalcified bone and temporal bones, eyes, placenta, hard or very fatty tissue, plus re-embedding/re-infiltration of blocks that processed poorly. Low volume, high skill, non-standard molds.

tasks.label: Cut sections of body tissues for microscopic examination, using microtomes.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Routine FFPE work in a hospital or reference histology lab: standard cassettes from larger specimens/resections (GI, GU, gyn, breast, lung), faced/trimmed then cut at 3-5 µm, ribbon floated and one section mounted per barcoded slide, dozens to hundreds of blocks per shift.

Small biopsy blocks (GI, skin punch/shave, prostate and breast cores, needle cores) with scant tissue: careful facing to avoid cutting through the specimen, multiple serial levels placed on one or several slides, often on urgent/express turnaround.

Recuts and extra unstained sections from already-faced archived blocks for IHC, special stains, molecular testing or slide replacement; block re-chilled/hydrated, several consecutive sections cut and mounted on charged slides.

Difficult or specialty paraffin blocks: decalcified or residually calcified bone, dense fibrous or heavily fatty tissue, curling or shattering blocks, oversized/mega whole-mount blocks; requires soaking, chilling, angle and orientation adjustment, re-embedding decisions.

Frozen sectioning on a cryostat: OCT-embedded fresh tissue for intraoperative consultation, Mohs margins, or immunofluorescence (renal/muscle biopsy); orienting and facing the frozen block, cutting 4-8 µm, picking sections up on slides within minutes.

Resin/plastic-embedded work in specialty or research labs: semithin toluidine-blue survey sections and ultrathin sections of epoxy-embedded tissue for electron microscopy, or serial sections for 3D reconstruction, collected on grids/tape/wafers.

instances.label: Routine H&E staining of formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded sections in a hospital or reference histology lab: racks of dried slides from microtomy are deparaffinized, stained through a graded reagent series, coverslipped, checked for nuclear/cytoplasmic contrast and floaters, and delivered to pathologist sign-out on daily turnaround.

Manual, judgement-dependent staining work: esoteric or endpoint-controlled stains (silver impregnations, hematoxylin differentiation checked under the microscope), de-coverslipping and restaining of unsatisfactory or faded slides, cytology smears/thick or decalcified sections, plus weighing/mixing/filtering dye solutions and qualifying new reagent lots against control slides.

instances.label: Routine daily case assembly in a hospital or reference histology lab: after coverslipping and drying, the histotech pulls each case's stained slides from staining/drying racks, checks each slide's label and count against the block list and requisition, sequences the slides in a folder or tray, attaches the requisition and the surgical working draft (gross description worksheet), and stages the completed case on the assigned pathologist's rack.

Paper packet compilation: printing the surgical working draft/gross worksheet, requisition, prior reports and consult forms from the LIS, collating them per case in the right order, and clipping the packet to the matching slide folder before sign-out.

Add-on materials for in-progress cases: recuts, levels, special stains, IHC and frozen-section slides ordered on cases already out for review; the tech matches the new slides to the open case, locates and updates the existing folder and its paperwork, and returns the augmented case to the ordering pathologist.

Distribution runs: carrying assembled case trays/folders from the histology lab to pathologists' offices, sign-out rooms, frozen-section room or another building/courier pickup point within the institution, with hand-off logging in the tracking system.

Archive and consult pulls: retrieving requested archived slides (and blocks) for outside consultation, tumor board, or a physician request; completing release paperwork and logs; packing slides with the forms in mailers for courier or mail shipment.

instances.label: Pathologist orders recuts/levels or additional unstained slides on a routine FFPE block after reviewing the initial H&E: histotech pulls the block from the file, faces/trims it, cuts 4-5 µm sections, floats and picks them up on labeled charged slides, dries, runs H&E on the automated stainer, coverslips, matches slides to the case, and returns them to the pathologist. Hospital/reference histology laboratory.

Pathologist orders an IHC panel (e.g., CK7/CK20/TTF-1, ER/PR/HER2) on a routine FFPE block: histotech cuts unstained charged slides plus on-slide or separate control tissue, labels/barcodes them per the LIS order, loads the automated IHC platform with the correct protocol, coverslips, checks controls for adequacy, and delivers stained slides within the ordered turnaround. Hospital/reference histology laboratory.

Pathologist orders histochemical special stains (PAS, PAS-D, GMS, trichrome, iron, AFB, mucicarmine, reticulin) on a routine FFPE block: histotech cuts sections plus positive controls, runs them on the automated special stainer (or by hand for stains not on the platform), coverslips, verifies control staining, and delivers. Hospital/reference histology laboratory.

Surgeon/pathologist requests an intraoperative frozen section: histotech receives fresh unfixed tissue of irregular size and consistency, orients and embeds it in OCT on a chuck, freezes, trims and cuts 4-6 µm sections in the cryostat, picks up sections on slides, performs rapid H&E, coverslips, and hands slides to the pathologist within ~15-20 minutes. Frozen-section room adjacent to the OR.

Pathologist orders a special preparation: direct immunofluorescence on a frozen renal or skin biopsy, decalcification and re-embedding of a bone/calcified specimen, glutaraldehyde/EM processing, or scraping/macrodissecting tumor-rich areas from unstained sections into tubes for a molecular send-out. Hospital/reference histology laboratory.

Order on a difficult or non-routine block, or a repeat after an unsatisfactory result: tiny needle-core or fatty/calcified/curled blocks needing hand facing, cold soaking and careful serial levels; re-embedding for correct orientation; or repeating a stain with an adjusted protocol after the pathologist rejects the first slide. Hospital/reference histology laboratory.

instances.label: Routine overnight run in a hospital/reference histology lab: after grossing, the histotech assembles grossed cassettes into processor baskets, loads them into an automated tissue processor (e.g., Sakura VIP 6, Leica PELORIS/PEGASUS), verifies/selects the dehydration-clearing-infiltration protocol on the touchscreen, starts the run, and unloads baskets next morning for embedding.

Same-day/rapid processing of small biopsies and urgent cases: cassettes of needle cores, endoscopic, GI and skin biopsies are loaded in batches through the day into a rapid microwave or continuous vacuum-infiltration processor; short protocol started, progress monitored, processed cassettes unloaded for immediate embedding.

Decalcification of bone/calcified specimens (bone marrow cores, bone chips, calcified vessels/valves): specimens in cassettes are loaded into a computerized decalcification/fixation unit or timed acid/EDTA protocol, protocol chosen by specimen type, endpoint checked, specimens rinsed and passed on to the tissue processor.

Keeping the computerized processing instruments running: verifying/rotating and replacing processing reagents and paraffin (5 L solvent bottles, wax pellets, waste), running cleaning and fill/drain cycles, and responding mid-run to alarms and faults (aborted run, clog, level error) including rescuing and re-processing affected specimens.

Specialty and research work in lower-volume labs: programmable processors for EM/resin or plastic-embedded specimens, research bone decalcification, and occasional microincineration/ashing of tissue for mineral/elemental examination, often under custom or newly evaluated protocols.

tasks.label: Prepare substances, such as reagents and dilution, and stains for histological specimens according to protocols.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Routine H&E / routine-stain bench setup in a hospital histology lab: filter or replace hematoxylin, top up eosin, bluing and differentiator, refresh graded alcohol and xylene baths, and charge the linear/autostainer reagent reservoirs (250 mL–1 L vessels), then date and label containers and log the change.

Special-stain / manual-stain reagent prep from powdered chemicals and stock acids (e.g., PAS Schiff, trichrome, silver, Congo red, iron stains): weigh mg–g on the analytical balance, dissolve in water/alcohol/acid, adjust pH, filter, aliquot into labeled 50–500 mL bottles, often in the fume hood, and record lot/expiry.

Bulk processing/fixation reagents: dilute 37% formaldehyde or concentrate to 10% neutral buffered formalin, make graded alcohols from absolute, prepare decal and clearing solutions in 5–20 L carboys, charge tissue-processor bulk stations and stain bulk containers, and handle/dispose of spent solvent.

Immunohistochemistry and special-technique working dilutions: pipette antibody concentrate into diluent at protocol ratios, prepare wash buffers and retrieval solutions from 10X concentrates or powders, aliquot into labeled vials, cap, mix, and store refrigerated with lot and expiry documentation.

Ad-hoc, research or new-protocol reagents: mounting media, fixatives, novel or literature-sourced stain recipes for a validation or research study; interpret a written protocol, source uncommon chemicals from storage, mix small trial batches, check pH/quality and document for the procedure manual.

tasks.label: Resolve problems with laboratory equipment and instruments, such as microscopes, mass spectrometers, microtomes, immunostainers, tissue processors, embedding centers, and water baths.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Microtome trouble at the cutting bench: sections show chatter/venetian blinding, ribbons won't form, or thickness is inconsistent. The histotechnologist diagnoses among blade nick/dullness, wrong clearance angle, loose block or blade-holder clamps, dried paraffin debris in the head, or a worn advance mechanism; changes or shifts the blade, re-torques or re-seats the holder, cleans wax/debris out of the mechanism, adjusts the angle, and re-cuts test sections until acceptable slides are produced.

Automated tissue processor fault in a hospital histology lab: an overnight run aborts or alarms (reagent level/valve error, blocked line, retort seal leak, paraffin solidified in a line, vacuum/pressure fault). The tech opens the retort, assesses whether tissue is at risk, drains/decants reagents, clears the blockage or replaces a seal/filter, runs a flush or cleaning cycle, restarts or reroutes the run to rescue the specimens, and documents the incident.

Automated immunostainer / special stainer / coverslipper problem: weak, absent, or uneven staining, dispense-probe clog, slide jam or misfeed, bulk-fluid or waste-line error, barcode read failure. The tech isolates instrument versus reagent versus protocol cause, primes/unclogs probes, clears jammed slides, replaces bulk containers or tubing, cleans wash stations, then reruns control slides and verifies staining quality before releasing patient work.

Support equipment problems: water/flotation bath temperature drift, scum or contaminated water; embedding center paraffin dispenser dripping or clogged nozzle, cold plate not chilling; paraffin oven or cryostat temperature/frost issues; cassette/slide printer jams; leaking reagent lines or hood alarm. The tech verifies with a calibrated thermometer, drains and cleans, clears the wax clog, adjusts the setpoint, and re-checks against QC limits.

Microscope and imaging equipment issues: poor illumination or uneven field, Köhler alignment lost, dirty or oil-contaminated objectives/condenser, failed bulb/LED, stage or focus drift; on a slide scanner, focus failures, tissue-detection errors, or dirty optics. The tech cleans optics with lens tissue and solvent, replaces the lamp, realigns illumination, and rescans/rechecks image quality.

Escalation and post-repair verification: fault cannot be resolved in-house, so the tech runs vendor-guided diagnostics over the phone, tags the instrument out of service, reroutes work to a backup instrument, hosts and assists the field service engineer, then performs post-service verification (calibration checks, control slides, temperature logs) and documents the corrective action for the QA record.

It shows machine control of blade and block handling, but the task here is fault diagnosis and physical remediation of malfunctioning instruments, which the system does not perform, so capability does not transfer.

It substantiates navigating and using instruments, but not fault diagnosis, disassembly, cleaning of internal fluidics, part replacement or post-repair verification, so it cannot substantiate this task.

tasks.label: Examine slides under microscopes to ensure tissue preparation meets laboratory requirements.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: High-volume routine QC of freshly stained and coverslipped H&E slides in a hospital or reference histology lab: the tech screens each slide at the microscope for section defects (folds, wrinkles, chatter, thick/thin sections), stain intensity and nuclear/cytoplasmic differentiation, coverslip bubbles/mounting defects, debris and floaters, and correct slide labeling, then passes the slide to the pathologist or returns it for restain/recut.

QC of histochemical special stains (trichrome, PAS, GMS, iron, reticulin) in the same lab: tech reviews the patient slide together with its stained control section to confirm the chemistry worked (correct color differentiation, no over/under-staining, clean background) before release.

QC of IHC/ISH slides: tech examines each immunostain with its positive/negative control tissue at the microscope, judging chromogen intensity, expected staining pattern/localization, counterstain, background and edge artifact, and decides accept vs repeat run.

Post-microtomy completeness and level checking: tech examines the stained sections microscopically to confirm the block is fully faced, all tissue pieces/levels requested are present and representative of the block, and orientation is correct, and issues recuts/deeper levels where they are not.

Intraoperative frozen-section QC in the frozen-section room adjacent to the OR: within a few minutes the tech checks the cryostat section under the scope for freeze/ice-crystal artifact, chatter, folds, incomplete face and stain adequacy, and recuts immediately if unsatisfactory while the surgeon waits.

QA program and troubleshooting review: tech examines slides microscopically to evaluate a new protocol, new antibody or reagent lot, a new instrument, or to diagnose a processing/staining fault (e.g., under-fixation, processor carryover), comparing against reference slides and documenting findings.

tasks.label: Prepare or use prepared tissue specimens for teaching, research or diagnostic purposes.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Routine diagnostic workload in a hospital or reference histology lab: a batch of formalin-fixed, cassetted specimens is processed, paraffin-embedded, trimmed and microtomed at 3-5 µm, sections floated and picked up on barcoded slides, dried/baked, H&E stained, coverslipped, QC'd and delivered to pathologists for sign-out within turnaround targets.

Diagnostic workup slides: cutting additional sections (and unstained/charged slides) from archived FFPE blocks and running special stains, IHC and ISH panels with positive/negative controls on automated platforms, then coverslipping, labeling and QC before release to the pathologist.

Specimen accession and grossing bench: receiving fixed specimens in jars (small GI/skin/prostate cores plus simple excisions), verifying identity against requisition, describing/measuring, inking or orienting where needed, and transferring tissue into labeled cassettes for processing.

Intraoperative frozen sections: fresh unfixed tissue arrives from the OR, is trimmed and oriented, embedded in OCT, snap-frozen on a chuck, sectioned on a cryostat, picked up on slides, rapidly stained and coverslipped, and delivered to the pathologist within about 15-20 minutes.

Research support in an academic or pharma/CRO histology lab: sectioning study FFPE blocks and building/sectioning tissue microarrays, running research IHC/IF or special stains per an investigator's protocol, with serial-section sets and documentation for the study.

Teaching and archival use of prepared specimens: pulling archived blocks/slides, cutting and staining duplicate teaching sets or conference/tumor-board slides, and digitizing prepared slides on a whole-slide scanner for teaching collections, research image sets or second opinions.

tasks.label: Perform procedures associated with histochemistry to prepare specimens for immunofluorescence or microscopy.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: High-volume routine histochemical special stains (PAS, PAS-D, Masson trichrome, GMS, iron, reticulin, Congo red, elastic) on batches of FFPE sections in a hospital or reference-lab histology suite: racking dried slides, loading reagent kits, running the protocol with positive control slides, rinsing, dehydrating, coverslipping and checking stain quality before release.

Immunofluorescence preparation on cryostat sections in a clinical immunopathology lab (renal biopsy DIF panel for IgG/IgA/IgM/C3/kappa/lambda, skin DIF, PGP9.5 nerve-fiber assay): air-drying, PBS washes, applying fluorophore-conjugated antisera, humid-chamber incubation, washing, aqueous anti-fade mounting and coverslipping, on a same-day clinical clock.

Immunohistochemistry / multiplex-immunofluorescence runs on FFPE surgical or biomarker cases prepared on an automated platform: dewaxing, heat or enzymatic antigen retrieval, blocking, primary and detection reagents, chromogen or fluorophore, counterstain, coverslip, with on-slide and control-tissue checks.

Bench preparation and QC of histochemical reagents and working solutions (weighing chemicals, dissolving to concentration, filtering, adjusting pH, labelling/dating) and verifying each fresh lot — e.g., silver or Warthin-Starry solutions — by staining control tissue and recording the result.

Non-routine or research histochemistry/IF: enzyme histochemistry on unfixed frozen muscle biopsy (NADH, SDH, COX, ATPase), whole-mount or thick-section immunofluorescence for confocal imaging, EM/resin specimen preparation, or optimizing a new stain by adjusting retrieval, dilution and incubation across repeat runs.
